activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Many ethicists distinguish doing harm from allowing harm, and most people judge causing a harm as worse than failing to prevent an equal harm, though some philosophers reject the distinction.
story:
Dominic had twenty minutes before the library closed, and the guilt was harder to carry than his backpack. He set the bag down carefully, as if the thing inside it might still be saved, and found Siena already installed at the corner table with her notes fanned out like a card trick.

"You look like you robbed a bank," she said.

"Worse." He unzipped the bag and lifted out Kaya's laptop, or the object that had been Kaya's laptop. The keyboard was stiff with juice, the residue of an energy drink he had knocked over during his shift at the cafe where they all worked. He had wiped the casing, closed it, and said nothing, and for two days the silence had sat in him like an encumbrance he couldn't set down. "She thinks the charger is broken. She ordered a new one."

Siena leaned back. "So you're going to confess to a librarian?"

"I'm going to look something up first." He had come for that reason, though he hadn't admitted it to himself until he said it aloud. In the ethics section he found a thin book about moral responsibility and stood in the aisle reading the way you check a diagnosis. The authors made a distinction he'd half-remembered from somewhere: many ethicists separate doing harm from allowing harm, and most people judge causing a harm as worse than failing to prevent an equal harm, though some philosophers reject the distinction entirely. He read the sentence twice, then a third time, because it seemed to be letting him off, and he didn't trust anything that convenient.

At dinner the week before, his father had slammed the salt down and declared that his uncle, who had watched a neighbor's porch steps rot and said nothing until the man fell, was as guilty as if he'd pushed him. His mother had called that absurd, and the argument had gone choleric fast, his father's voice rising until the plates seemed to sublimate the anger into a fine vibrating hum. Dominic had pushed his food around and said nothing, which, given what he now carried in his backpack, was its own small irony. Even then, some part of him had understood that the argument wasn't really about the uncle. It was about what you owed people when you had simply watched.

He carried the book back to the table. "Here's the thing," he said to Siena, opening it between them. "Causing a harm versus allowing one. Most people think causing it is worse, even if the harm's the same size. Some philosophers think the whole distinction is fake." He tapped the page. "I caused this one. I didn't just watch it happen."

"And that matters why?"

"Because if I let her keep believing it's the charger, I'm doing a second thing on top of the first. The spill was an accident. This part wouldn't be." He hadn't planned to say it that plainly, but the library's hush made plainness feel possible, the way confession booths probably did for people who had them. "There were trade-offs either way. Tell her and she's furious and I probably pay for it and my shifts get weird for a month. Don't tell her and I get to keep my reputation, which I didn't earn."

Siena considered this with the seriousness she gave everything, which was why he'd come to her table instead of hiding at home. "So what's the solution?"

He told her: he'd found a repair shop near the bus station that replaced keyboards the same day, and he had his savings from the cafe, and if Kaya came in tomorrow he could hand the laptop back working before she ever discovered the truth. But he'd also tell her, exactly, what had happened, because the fix without the confession was just a cleaner version of the silence. "I want both parts. The repair and the truth." He paused. "I still don't know if the doing-versus-allowing thing actually holds up. Maybe my dad's right and watching is just as bad. But I know which one I did."

Behind them, a voice said, "The library closes in ten minutes." It was Ms. Mensah, resettling returns onto her cart, and her eye fell on the open book. "Ethics in the spring. You must be the one who wrote the essay about the trolley problem."

"I got it wrong," Dominic said. "You wrote that in the margin."

She smiled slightly and pushed her cart on. "Get it wrong differently next time."

He closed the book, zipped the laptop into the bag, and at the door his phone buzzed: Kaya, with a photo of a package. "Charger came," her message read. "Laptop still dead though. Weird. Bringing it to the library tomorrow, Ms. Mensah knows a guy."

Dominic stood on the steps in the last of the light, thumb hovering, and typed: "Actually, bring it to me first. I know what happened."

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: In 2011 the OPERA experiment reported neutrinos apparently faster than light; in 2012 the result was traced to a loose fibre-optic cable, and other experiments measured speeds consistent with light.
story:
Adrian burst through the door of the science classroom waving his phone like a hall pass that could get him anywhere, and Antoine, who had been quietly titrating a pale pink solution at the back bench and had reached the exact drop where one more would ruin everything, set the burette down with exaggerated care. "Einstein is finished," Adrian announced. "They measured these particles going faster than light. Neutrinos. It's the OPERA experiment, 2011, it's huge." Imogen, who sat nearest the window and rarely looked up before the second bell, looked up.

The whole thing annoyed Antoine more than it should have, and he told himself the annoyance was about accuracy, not about the fact that Adrian had once again arrived first at something. Last year Adrian had found the summer program, the one with the telescopes, and had mentioned it casually a week after applications closed. That was a separate matter, Antoine reminded himself. Completely separate. He was thinking only of the truth.

"Which experiment," he asked, and Adrian showed him the headline, which said exactly what Adrian had said, only with more exclamation points.

"One result," Antoine said.

"One result that broke relativity."

"Remember when we did that thing in class," Antoine said, "where Mr. Villanueva had three groups measure the same block of sedimentary rock and we all got different densities, and it turned out Jessica's balance had a thumbprint on the pan?" He had not thought about that day in months, and it surfaced now with an odd clarity, the afternoon light, the smudge on the metal, the smallness of the cause. Imogen said, "That's not the same thing."

"I know it's not the same thing," Antoine said, though a voice in his head, one he preferred not to listen to, said he was only pretending to be the reasonable one, that being the reasonable one was his own performance, his own headline.

Mr. Villanueva came in then with his coffee and his stack of photocopies, and Antoine decided not to ask him. Partly this was strategy; if he asked an adult, the answer would belong to the adult, and Antoine wanted the answer to be his, wanted to walk in tomorrow with something Adrian did not have. Partly it was pride. Mostly, if he was honest, and he was trying to be honest, it was both at once, and he could not titrate them apart.

That night he did not start with the headline. He started with the experiment's name, which Adrian had given him like a gift he didn't know he was giving, and he went looking not for excitement but for what came after. It took longer than he expected, partly because there was so much celebration online, so many pages still glowing with the news of physics overturned, a whole veneer of triumph laid over the underlying question nobody wanted to sit with. But underneath it, in quieter places, he found the rest. Other experiments had gone looking. And in 2012 the original result had been traced to a loose fibre-optic cable. A cable. A connection not quite seated in its socket. Other experiments measured the neutrinos' speeds consistent with light, and the world went back to its old shape.

He sat with that for a while, the screen's glow on his hands, feeling two things at once and unwilling to give up either. One was the flat disappointment of the mundane explanation, a wire, a thumbprint, the universe refusing to be interesting on demand. The other was something he had no good word for, something almost like relief: that one result, however dazzling, was not the same as knowledge. That knowledge was the thing that survived being checked. He thought about how quickly he had wanted to correct Adrian, and how the correction itself would have been, if he had made it yesterday, made of nothing, just a hunch and a dislike dressed up as skepticism.

The next morning he found Adrian at the bench before class, arranging his phone face down like a card he was saving. "I looked it up," Antoine said.

"Of course you did."

"In 2012 they found it was a loose fibre-optic cable. The faster-than-light result. And other experiments measured speeds consistent with light." He said it flatly, without triumph, and was surprised at how much effort the flatness took, because a part of him wanted to lay it down like a winning hand, wanted Adrian to feel the exact size of it.

Adrian picked up his phone, put it down again. "So Einstein's fine."

"Einstein's fine."

"That's disappointing," Adrian said, but he was smiling a little, the way he did when he'd been caught being wrong about something that didn't cost him anything. Then he frowned. "Wait. Did you find that out to prove me wrong, or because you actually wanted to know?"

The question was fair, and Antoine had been asking himself a version of it since the night before, without a clean answer. There had been wanting-to-win in it, undeniably, and there had also been the thing underneath, the thing about thumbprints and cables and the patience of checking. He opened his mouth, and Imogen, arriving with her bag over one shoulder, said, "Don't answer that, it's a trap." Mr. Villanueva was writing on the board in his slow, careful hand, and the first bell rang, and Adrian turned around in his seat, and Antoine picked up the burette and gave the pink solution one more drop.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that everyone aged 13 to 64 be tested for HIV at least once as part of routine health care.
story:
Rachel had volunteered for the health hut because it came with a free week of camp and a laminated badge with her name on it, and she had kept volunteering after the badge stopped being the point. The training happened in the mornings, before the heat, in a screened room behind the infirmary where Mr. Pham, the camp nurse, kept a shelf of pamphlets and a bowl of expired latex gloves that trainees practiced putting on and taking off without snapping. By the second Thursday she could list the methods of contraception on a whiteboard in an order that was supposed to feel casual, the way a menu lists the day's specials, and she could say the word condom to a circle of fifteen-year-olds without her voice climbing an octave.

Consent was harder, and everyone in the training knew it. Mr. Pham had given them a single sheet of principles and then said, in his unhurried way, that the sheet was the easy part. Rachel's job that afternoon was to run a practice session for two other trainees, Calleigh and Katelynn, who sat on opposite ends of a picnic table under the awning, one attentive and one radiating the particular boredom of a person who had been sent somewhere by her mother.

"Okay," Rachel said. "Somebody give me a situation where somebody changes their mind halfway through something."

Katelynn looked at the lake. "Eating a whole canoe," she said.

"Fine. Eating a whole canoe. And then what does the other person do?"

"Stop feeding them the canoe."

The joke landed somewhere in the middle of the table and stayed there, and Rachel let it, because it was closer to the lesson than the sheet was. She talked about duress, using the word the way Mr. Pham had used it, quietly, as though it were only one kind of pressure among many: a ride home that's been offered, an audience, a favor being called in. She had practiced the line the night before in her bunk, whispering it to the mosquito netting. Saying it out loud to two actual people made it sound thinner, and she slowed down and said more of it, which was better.

Calleigh, who wanted to be a nurse and organized her flashcards the way other people organized grudges, kept trying to prognosticate, to run every scenario forward to its worst outcome and grade it. "But what if they say yes because they're scared of what happens if they say no," she said, and Rachel said that wasn't consent either, and Calleigh nodded and wrote it down and looked briefly satisfied, which Rachel had learned not to trust as a sign of anything.

The part Rachel had not expected to be the easy part was the clinic piece, and that was because of the physical she'd had in June, three days before staff week. She'd gone in for a sports form, expecting a stethoscope and a stamp. The doctor had offered her an HIV test, and Rachel had laughed, because she'd assumed it meant the doctor suspected something, and the doctor had said no, it's routine, the CDC recommends everyone aged 13 to 64 get tested at least once as part of routine health care, and did she want it today. Rachel had said yes mostly out of politeness, and had sat with the strange privacy of the finger stick, and had thought about the number 64 for the rest of the appointment, about a person getting tested who was older than her grandfather.

"So it's not a punishment," she told Calleigh and Katelynn now, holding up the pamphlet she'd kept folded in her backpack all summer, its creases gone soft. "It's like blood pressure. You don't get your blood pressure taken because someone thinks you did something." Katelynn, who had been carving her initials into the table with a thumbnail, stopped. She said her cousin had cried in a parking lot last spring because a clinic had asked her questions like that, and everyone had treated it like a confession.

"It's a recommendation for everyone," Rachel said. "Thirteen to sixty-four. At least once. That's the whole thing." She had thought about how to say it for a week, whether it would land as reassurance or as a statistic, and this was the sentence she'd settled on, and she delivered it and then made herself stop talking, because the training binder had a line in it that said let silence do some of the work, and until that moment she'd thought it was a typing error.

Katelynn said, quietly, that maybe she'd get tested at her physical in August, then, since it was just routine, and asked Rachel whether the clinic in her town did walk-ins. Rachel said she didn't know, that she'd only ever been a patient and never the person explaining it, and that she could find out. Katelynn nodded and went back to the lake with her eyes but not with her shoulders, which had dropped an inch.

After the session, Mr. Pham collected the whiteboard markers and asked how it had gone, and Rachel started to prognosticate, to list what she'd gotten wrong, and then stopped herself mid-word. She told him the consent part still felt like carrying water in her hands, that she could get it across the room but not without losing some, and that she didn't know yet whether the losing was the failure or just the nature of the carrying. He considered that while he capped a marker, and said only, "Same time tomorrow."

That night Rachel sat on the infirmary steps with the pamphlet, reading the clinic's hours by the light of the doorway, and Calleigh came out with two popsicles from the freezer and handed her one without being asked.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In his Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle described each virtue as a mean between two extremes; courage, for example, lies between cowardice and recklessness.
story:
The morning of the regional debate final, Justin found Elliott alone in the empty rehearsal room, copying cards. He had been planning what to say for two days, ever since he learned that Elliott had used an article Myriam found and never told her, folding her research into his rebuttal as though he had dug it out himself.

"You took her migration data," Justin said. He kept his voice level, which took effort, because his hands wanted to shake the cards right out of Elliott's grip.

Elliott looked up, and for a second his face was naked with panic before the composure came down over it, diaphanous and unconvincing. "It's a team effort. We share everything."

"She asked you where you got it. Twice. And you told her the library database didn't log searches." That part had stung Justin most, the small clean subterfuge of it, a lie so tidy it could pass for a technicality.

"I'll credit her after we win." Elliott squared the cards against the desk. "If I stop to renegotiate the deck an hour before the final, we lose. Is that what you want? You want to lose regionals over a footnote?"

Justin hadn't come in with an answer to that. He had come in with the hot certainty that silence would make him complicit, and now the certainty was draining out of him and leaving something enervating in its place, a tiredness that came from holding two truths at once. Winning mattered. Myriam mattered. He stood there while the clock on the wall ticked toward round one.

Ms. Foster found him in the corridor a few minutes later, carrying the ballot sheets. "You look like a man who lost his own argument," she said, and kept walking, which was her way of leaving a door open.

In the prep room, Myriam sat with her laptop open and her posture closed, shoulders curled inward as if against a draft only she could feel. Justin sat down across from her. "I know about the data," he said. "I know he claimed the database search. I'm going to say something to him in front of the coach if he doesn't say it first."

"You'll blow up the team an hour before the final." She said it without heat, which was worse than anger. "I already did the math on that. I lose either way. Either I'm the girl who got used, or I'm the girl who torpedoed regionals."

That was when the thing he'd read in October came back to him, a passage he'd marked because it sounded elegant rather than because he'd needed it. He turned his chair to face her fully. "You remember that ethics packet Ms. Foster gave us? Aristotle, the Nicomachean Ethics. He said each virtue is a mean between two extremes. Courage sits between cowardice and recklessness."

"So?"

"So maybe I've been thinking there are only two moves. Say nothing, which is cowardice, or confront him in front of everyone right before we go on, which might just be recklessness with a righteous label on it. Maybe the actual brave thing is somewhere in between." He heard how the words sounded as he said them, like a debater testing a case, and he was honest enough to wince at it. "I don't know where the middle is. I'm guessing. But guessing in a direction beats flipping a coin between two extremes."

Myriam closed the laptop halfway, thinking. "The coach checks the source log at five. If Elliott's name is on a card he can't source, the coach asks him. Then it's not a confrontation, it's a question."

The final round began at four. Justin argued his parts cleanly, and when Elliott stood for rebuttal, he opened his mouth, paused, and then said, almost in passing, "Building on the sourcing our team developed together, particularly Myriam's database work, which the judges will find in appendix B." It was not an apology. It was a sentence with a trapdoor in it, and everyone on their side of the table knew what had fallen through. Myriam's shoulders came down an inch. Justin caught her eye across the aisle and she gave him the smallest nod, the kind that means the debt is registered, not yet paid.

They took second place. Afterward, in the parking lot, the light going amber over the buses, Myriam said, "The middle. You found a middle that wasn't mine and wasn't his."

"I think I found one middle for one afternoon," Justin said. "I still don't know what I'd do next time." He said it plainly, because it was true, and because he had learned, somewhere between October and this hour, that a position you can't revise isn't a position at all, it's just a wall.

She shouldered her bag. "Appendix C, then," she said. "We'll write the next one together."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: In Peter Wason's 1966 selection task, people must pick which cards to turn over to test an if-then rule; in his study, fewer than 10 percent chose the correct cards in the abstract version.
story:
Ms. Farah set four cards on the document camera before the bell had even finished: K, 4, A, 7. "Each card has a letter on one face and a number on the other," she said. "Here is a rule. If a card has a K on one side, then it has a 4 on the other. Write down which cards you must turn over to test the rule. Only the ones you must."

Charles wrote K and 4, then second-guessed himself and crossed out the 4, then wrote it again. Around him, pens scratched. Kiptyn was already leaning back with his arms folded, which meant he thought he was done and right. The only sound for a minute was the radiator ticking.

"K and 7," said Darien when Ms. Farah called on him. "You have to see if the K has a 4, and you have to see what's behind the 7, because if it's a K back there, the rule's dead."

Kiptyn snorted. "The 7 doesn't matter. The rule says K implies 4. It doesn't say anything about 7s." He'd been building this argument since sophomore year, since debate club gave him a vocabulary for winning: the antecedent, the consequent, the contrapositive, all of it delivered with a fluency that made disagreement feel like clumsiness. His oratory had a way of filling a room so completely that quieter answers stopped being offered at all.

Ms. Farah wrote the two answers side by side, K and 4 versus K and 7, and said only, "This is the selection task, from Peter Wason, 1966. He ran the abstract version, just letters and numbers like these, and fewer than 10 percent of his subjects picked the correct cards." She would not say which side was right. She tapped the board once and moved on to attendance, which was her way of leaving a grenade on the table.

Charles found it unbearable. At lunch he carried his tray past the usual table and sat with his notebook open, drawing four rectangles over and over. The K had to be turned; everyone agreed on that; if its back wasn't a 4, the rule was false. The 4 was tempting but useless, because the rule never claimed that only Ks had 4s. He could hear Kiptyn saying it, and Kiptyn was right about that part. But the 7. He drew a 7 with a hidden K behind it, and something shifted in his chest, the same feeling as when a proof folded shut in geometry. A 7 with a K behind it would break the rule just as thoroughly as a K with something else behind it. Turning the 4 was looking for more agreement; turning the 7 was hunting for the thing that could prove you wrong. Darien had seen it in one pass. Darien, who never ran for student council, who lost words in front of crowds, had gone straight for the disconfirming case.

He found Darien at his locker after last period. "You were right," Charles said. "The 7. I had the 4." Darien shrugged, pulling out a chemistry binder, but his ears had gone slightly red. "It's easier to look for reasons you're right," Darien said. "Harder to look for the card that might call you a liar." Charles laughed, and then didn't, because it wasn't funny exactly. He thought of Kiptyn's undefeated record, of how it was built, match by match, out of arguments stacked on the side that flattered him. It was a pernicious kind of winning, the kind you couldn't see the cost of because the cost was everything you never turned over.

But he couldn't internalize it cleanly either, and that bothered him all through dinner. If hunting for disproof made people right, why did almost nobody do it, and why had Charles needed half a day and a notebook? And Kiptyn wasn't a fool; in round two of the debate finals last spring, Kiptyn had attacked his own case before the other team could, which was the same move Darien had made with the 7. Maybe the difference wasn't honesty but practice, and maybe it only worked when the stakes were cards on a table instead of things you wanted.

The next morning Charles stopped at Kiptyn's locker before homeroom, the notebook page folded in his hand. "Do it for real," he said, holding it out. "Take the rule, tell me which cards you'd turn." Kiptyn took the page and looked at it for a long moment, longer than he ever looked at anything, and Charles watched his thumb rest on the corner of the paper, not quite turning it over.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many Orthodox churches, including the Russian Orthodox Church, celebrate Christmas on January 7 because they keep December 25 on the older Julian calendar.
story:
The cultural center smelled of pine and fried dough, and Daniel stood near the coat rack holding his grandmother's mended shawl while she hugged a stream of people he half recognized. The hall had been decorated the night before, garlands strung along the windows, a tree in the corner still waiting for its ornaments. Outside, the January light was thin and boreal, the kind that made the parking lot look like a photograph of itself. His grandmother had been clear on the drive over: he was to help, he was to be pleasant, and he was not to mention what had happened at school before the break.

What had happened at school was this. In December, Randy had asked him what he was doing for Christmas, and Daniel, who had grown tired of explaining, had said nothing. He and his family were nothing, as far as Randy needed to know. It was easier than the truth, which involved his grandmother's church and a date that made his classmates laugh when Gael once brought it up in the cafeteria. "Two weeks late," Gael had said, grinning. "Even the calendar is wrong." Daniel had let it go. He had let it go for two years.

Now his grandmother pressed a box of glass ornaments into his hands and pointed him toward the tree. He hung them carefully, one at a time, and found Mr. Lau already there, untangling a string of lights with the patience of a man who had done it many times. Mr. Lau lived three doors down and came to the center every year, though Daniel had never worked out why. "Hold this end," Mr. Lau said, and Daniel did. When the lights came on, the tree seemed to transfigure, the glass catching small red and gold fires, and a few of the younger children stopped their running to stare at it.

A boy about nine years old, one of the Sunday school kids, tugged at Daniel's sleeve. "My friend at school says we don't even have Christmas," the boy said. "He says it's still coming. But we already had it. Didn't we?"

Daniel opened his mouth to say something reassuring, and then closed it, because the honest answer was stranger than that. "We keep December twenty-fifth," he said slowly, hearing his grandmother's phrasing come out of him, "just on the old Julian calendar. So for us it lands on January seventh." The boy frowned, and Daniel remembered his grandmother saying the words last year, standing at this same tree. "The Russian Orthodox Church never changed over," she had said. "So our Christmas comes after the neighbors'." That was all she had ever said about it. He had looked up the rest himself, late at night, hunched over his phone.

"Is that bad?" the boy asked.

"No," Daniel said. "It's just ours." But even as he said it, he felt the older answer rise in him, the one he'd worn at school like a coat: nothing, we're nothing, don't ask. Gael's word for it, he thought, would have been something clever and unkind, the kind of dysphemism that makes a whole tradition sound like a mistake. Daniel had never corrected it. He had preferred being laughed at to being explained.

Later, when the tables were set and the carols had started, he found his phone in his pocket and, without quite deciding to, opened a message to Randy. He typed that he'd been at his grandmother's Christmas today, January seventh, because her church kept the old calendar, and that the things he'd said before were wrong. He looked at the message for a long time. Around him people were singing in a language he only half knew, and Mr. Lau was humming along anyway, following the melody rather than the words, which seemed to Daniel like its own kind of belonging. The tree glowed in the corner. Somewhere near the kitchen his grandmother was laughing at something.

He didn't know whether Randy would care, or whether it would change anything at school, or whether being honest about one thing obligated him to be honest about everything. He pressed send anyway, then slid the phone back into his pocket and went to find his grandmother. She was ladling punch into paper cups, and when he reached her she handed him one without a word, and together they stood listening to the singing, the two of them and the whole warm room, while outside the boreal afternoon deepened into blue.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under joint and several liability, each of several people who share an obligation can be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share.
story:
The cursor blinked in the signature field, thin and patient, and Alexis moved the mouse away from it as if the small gesture could postpone the decision. The lease sat open on his laptop in the kitchen, forty-one pages of it, though only the last page mattered tonight. Alice had texted twice already: just sign it, the apartment is going fast. Natalya had said the same thing more quietly, in a voice message from the stairwell of her building, traffic hissing behind her words.

He had told them he would sign after dinner, and then he had not eaten dinner. Instead he scrolled upward through the document the way his mother rinsed a glass twice, not because the first rinse failed but because the second cost nothing. Most of it had the texture of language designed never to be read: herein, whereas, the party of the first part. Somewhere around page nine his attention began to coagulate around a paragraph he had skimmed three times without catching, and on the fourth pass he stopped skimming.

Joint and several liability. The words sat in the middle of a long sentence, unremarkable in their font, and he read the sentence aloud in the empty kitchen to hear how it worked. Each tenant, the lease said, would be responsible for the full rent, not merely his or her portion. He read it again. His share was nine hundred a month. The whole rent was twenty-seven hundred. If Alice went to grad school in Scotland and Natalya's job folded, the number that would arrive in his inbox was twenty-seven hundred, every month, for twelve months.

He opened a new tab and typed the phrase into the search bar, half expecting the internet to soften what the lease had said. It did not. Every result agreed. Under joint and several liability, each of several people who share an obligation can be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share. A forum thread from three years ago described a man whose roommates had vanished in October; the landlord had pursued him through the following August, and the thread ended without saying how it ended.

Alexis leaned back. The refrigerator hummed its one note, and through the window the streetlight made a small yellow coin on the counter beside the keyboard. He was not angry at Alice or Natalya. That was the strange part. He could see the whole thing from the landlord's side, could see why a person renting to three eighteen-year-olds would want three doors to knock on instead of one. And he could see it from theirs, the way they had divided the rooms and the utilities in Alice's car that night, laughing, the map on Natalya's phone glowing between the seats. Both views were reasonable. They simply did not fit in the same frame, and the lease was the frame.

He called Alice. She picked up on the second ring, a television murmuring behind her.

"Did you read the liability part?" he asked.

"The what?"

"Page nine. If one of us doesn't pay, the others owe everything. It's called joint and several liability. Each of us could owe the whole rent, not just our share."

There was a pause in which the television said something about weather. "That's standard," Alice said. "Every lease has it. My cousin said so."

Her cousin was twenty-three and lived at home, but Alexis did not say this. Instead he asked whether she had read page nine herself, and she admitted, in a smaller voice, that she had signed the digital copy already, at the coffee shop, on her phone, with her thumb. Natalya had done the same an hour later. He looked at the tab still open behind the call screen, the field with the blinking cursor, the document waiting for him the way documents do, without opinion.

"Ask them for a guarantor clause," he said finally. "Or separate leases. Or a cap. I don't know yet what they'll agree to, but I'm not signing this version tonight."

"You're going to lose the apartment."

"Then I lose the apartment." He heard how it sounded and softened it. "I'll email the agent in the morning. If they won't change a word, we'll find out what we're each willing to risk, all three of us, on the same page."

Alice was quiet for a moment, and then the television went off. "Send me page nine," she said. "I'll read it on the laptop, not the phone."

He told her he would, and after they hung up he did not close the tab. He copied the paragraph into a message, pasted it twice more, once for Alice and once for Natalya, and sat looking at the cursor, still blinking, patient as ever, in a field he had decided would stay empty for one more night. Outside, a car passed, and the yellow coin of streetlight slid off the counter and onto his hand.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back in student housing found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends.
story:
The moving truck left tire prints in the fresh asphalt of Halden Court, which was so new that half the lawns were still dirt and the saplings along the curb were staked like patients. Julia sat on the porch steps with her phone warm in her hand, rereading the group chat from her old town until the screen dimmed. Nour had written, you'll make friends in a week, you always do, and Kylan had sent a row of exclamation points, as if enthusiasm could be transferred like a file. She wanted to believe them, and she also wanted to know whether believing them was the same as it being true.

The boxes in her room had been labeled by her mother in a shorthand Julia couldn't crack. One marked MISC turned out to be mostly her father's old college textbooks, and she stacked them on the windowsill to get them out of the way. The top one was a sociology reader with a cracked spine, and when it flopped open, a page had been dog-eared years ago. She read it standing up, one hip against the windowsill, because something in it snagged on her situation. In 1950, three researchers named Festinger, Schachter and Back had studied student housing, and they found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends. Not people with matching hobbies. Not people with compatible personalities. People whose doors happened to be near each other.

She carried the book downstairs and out to the porch, where a man was trimming the hedge of the house next door. He introduced himself as Mr. Esposito, said he'd lived on the court since before the bulldozers came, and offered her a glass of lemonade as though they'd known each other for a decade. She asked him whether he was friends with the people closest to him. "The Ferraros, two doors down, we talk every day," he said. "The family at the end of the court, couldn't tell you their dog's name." He squinted at her. "Why do you ask?" She showed him the dog-eared page. He read it slowly, moving his lips, and handed it back. "Distance," he said. "Half the stuff we call chemistry is just geography." She liked that, and wrote it in her notebook, though she wasn't sure it was entirely fair.

The question that kept her awake was whether the finding was a comfort or a sentence. If proximity made friends, then leaving her old town had cost her something no amount of texting could resuscitate. Her friendships with Nour and Kylan had been built in hallways and bus seats, in the accidental architecture of a schedule, and now she'd been picked up and set down miles from all of it. But the same fact meant that the girl in the house across the court, the one she'd seen carrying in a desk chair by herself, was statistically her next friend, whoever she happened to be. Both readings were true at once, and Julia lay in the dark turning them over like two stones of the same weight.

On Monday she started at the school two neighborhoods over, where nobody knew her and the hallways smelled of floor wax and unfamiliar shampoo. At lunch she found herself in the library instead of the cafeteria, telling herself she preferred it. But the study nagged at her. She was not near shared stairways here; she was nowhere at all, a kid who took her food to a quiet room. So on Tuesday she forced herself into the cafeteria and took the empty seat at the end of a table, close to a boy named Kylan, no relation to her Kylan except the coincidence of the name, which she found almost funny. He was doing a crossword with a virtuoso's speed, pen only, no erasing, and when she said the answer to seven across was "manatee," he slid the puzzle toward her without a word.

By Thursday they had a system: she took the even clues, he took the odd ones, and a girl named Nour from his chemistry class had drifted into the third chair, apparently because it was the third chair. Nour said she'd only started sitting there two weeks ago. "I used to eat in the art room," she said, peeling an orange. "Then one day I just didn't feel like walking that far." Julia felt something click into place, quiet and satisfying. She thought about the stairways in the 1950 study, the doors near doors, and about how friendship might be less like a treasure hunt and more like weather, something that forms where conditions happen to converge. She still didn't know whether that made friendship less meaningful or more, and she suspected she'd be arguing with herself about it for a while.

That weekend the court was friable with drought, the dirt lawns crumbling to powder underfoot, and Julia walked to the end of the sidewalk to where the girl from across the street was struggling with a basketball net in her driveway. The pole leaned at a tired angle, and a screw rolled off the backboard and landed in the dust. Julia picked it up and held it out. "You need someone to hold this while you tighten it?" The girl looked at her for a second, then wiped her hands on her shorts. "Actually yeah," she said. "Hold it steady. I'm Priya."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: In Java, a field marked private can be read or changed only by code inside the same class.
story:
The router at his grandfather's house still blinked amber, so Alexis carried his laptop out to the kitchen table where the light was better anyway. His grandfather sat at the far end with the newspaper folded to the crossword, working a pen across the squares in small decisive strokes. The assignment was due Sunday night: build a Java class with private fields and getter methods, then test it. Alexis had read the chapter twice on the bus and understood approximately none of it, which was, he told himself, why he was here rather than at home, where the wifi worked and his mother would ask how it was going.

He typed the class first, because that much he could copy from his notes. A class called Book, with fields for title and pages. He made the fields private because the instructions said to, the same way he put on a seatbelt: a rule whose reasons were somebody else's business. Then he opened a second file for the test, and in it he wrote the obvious thing, the thing his hands wanted to write, which was to print the title straight out.

The compiler refused. It underlined the line in red and offered a message he read three times: Book has private access, it said, in the flat tone of a customs officer denying entry. Alexis sat back. He looked at the underline the way you look at a door that has always been open and now, for reasons of its own, is not.

His phone buzzed on the table. It was Matis, who had finished the assignment on Thursday, because Matis finished everything on Thursday, and who had taken to ending his messages with long mock-heroic speeches about his own discipline. The latest one arrived in installments, and Alexis scrolled to the end of the peroration, which concluded that Matis would be a senior engineer by twenty-five and Alexis was welcome to watch. Alexis typed: my test won't compile. It says Book has private access. What does that even mean.

Matis replied with a single line, no commentary, which for him was remarkable: "Private means the field can be read or changed only by code inside the same class." Alexis read it twice. The class could touch its own fields; the test, living in a different file, a different class, could not. It was not an error, then. It was the point.

He sat with that for a moment, turning his pen over. He thought of Grant, who had abandoned computer science in October and become briefly disaffected, telling anyone who would listen that programming was just bureaucracy with worse lighting. Alexis had half agreed at the time. But this felt less like bureaucracy and more like the hallway of his grandfather's house, where certain doors, the one to the old sewing room, the one to the cellar, simply were not for guests, and everyone understood this without a sign being posted. The class kept its own counsel. If you wanted the title, you had to ask the class for it.

So he wrote a getter, a small method called getTitle that lived inside Book and handed the title back out. He called it from the test. It compiled, and the console printed the title in plain gray text, and Alexis felt something loosen in his chest that he had not noticed tightening. He wrote a getter for pages too. Then, feeling bolder, he wrote a setter that refused to accept a page count of zero, and when the test tried it, the old value stayed. He had not been asked to do that. It had simply occurred to him that a class guarding its fields might also judge what they were asked to hold.

The neighbor, Mr. Lewandowski, knocked at four with a casserole dish his grandfather had apparently won from him at cards, and the two of them stood in the doorway conducting the handover with the ceremony of a border exchange. Alexis closed his laptop halfway to be polite. Mr. Lewandowski asked what he was working on, and Alexis found himself explaining it, the private fields, the getters, the test outside looking in, and heard his own voice grow more certain as he went, the way it did when he was arguing a position he had only just discovered he held. It was not only a rule to obey, he said. It was also a way of thinking: you decided what belonged inside, and what the outside got to see, and those were two different decisions.

Mr. Lewandowski said it sounded like the opposite of how he had run his restaurant kitchen, where everything was visible to everybody, and Alexis said that might be exactly the trade. He was not sure, actually, whether hiding things made code better or only made it safer, whether the wall was discipline or just fear of other people's mistakes, and he said so, because Mr. Lewandowski was the kind of adult who did not mind an unfinished thought. His grandfather, listening from his chair, only said that in his day you kept things private because there was no other way to keep them honest.

That evening, after the casserole and the crossword had both been finished, Alexis ran the test file one more time. Six green checkmarks. He almost wrote to Matis, to report the score and thereby exculpate himself for the afternoon of struggle, but he closed the message window instead, deciding the green marks could speak for themselves. He saved both files, wiped the crumbs from the table with the edge of his sleeve, and carried the laptop back down the hall toward the amber light, where the router was still blinking and his grandfather was turning off lamps, one room at a time.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Freezing food at -18 degrees Celsius (0 degrees Fahrenheit) stops bacteria from growing but does not kill most of them, so thawed food can spoil again.
story:
Justin's mother had been home from the hospital for six days, convalescing on the couch with a stack of novels she wasn't reading, and his father had appointed him, by default, the person who fed the household. His cooking so far had been pasta on Monday, pasta on Tuesday, and toast. On Wednesday his mother handed him a bank card and said the word "planning" twice, the way she said most important things, as if repetition could substitute for demonstration.

So on Saturday morning he stood at the entrance to the farmers' market with a folded piece of paper in his back pocket, a list written the night before after an hour of scrolling through recipes he mostly didn't trust. He had landed on a plan he thought he could survive: a pot of lentil soup, a tray of baked chicken and potatoes, a chili, and rice in bulk. Cook everything Sunday, portion it, eat it through the week. It was the interregnum between his mother's kitchen and whatever he would do at college in two years, and he intended to fill it with something better than takeout.

Arman was already inside, leaning over a crate of tomatoes, and Zaina appeared ten minutes later with her own canvas bag, because she came to this market every week and had opinions about which stalls were honest. She steered him away from the first onion seller without explaining, then explained anyway: that guy weighed with his thumb on the scale. Arman carried Justin's list for him and read it aloud in a talk-show voice, "Six potatoes, one kilogram of lentils, dignity," until Zaina took the paper back.

The cooking itself went better than he expected and worse than the recipes promised. The chili took two hours, not forty minutes, because he'd put the onions in before the pan was hot and then stood there scraping brown glue off the bottom. The soup was fine. By Sunday night the counter held seven containers, and he stood over them with the freezer door open, tired in a way that felt almost like accomplishment.

That was when the trouble started. One container of chili, the last spooned out, had sat on the counter while he ate dinner, maybe three hours, and then he'd put it in the freezer anyway. He reasoned it out while wiping down the stove: the freezer would fix it. Cold killed things, that was the whole point of refrigeration, and a freezer was just refrigeration with more conviction. He stacked the containers and shut the door.

Monday he mentioned it to Arman at the lunch table, casually, as a note about his weekend, and Arman set down his sandwich. "You left it out and then froze it? That's not how it works. Freezing food at minus eighteen degrees, zero Fahrenheit, stops bacteria from growing, but it doesn't kill most of them. Thawed food can spoil again." He said it flatly, like a fact he'd had to memorize for a food-safety unit in health class and had never expected to deploy. "Whatever grew in those three hours is still in there."

Justin argued for a minute, because the alternative was throwing food away, and the whole point of the project had been to not waste the money from the market. But the argument collapsed quickly. Zaina, who had drifted over, put it more bluntly: bacteria aren't like us, they don't mind waiting. He thought about the container, third from the top, with its film of orange fat already congealing, and about his mother on the couch, whose whole body was currently occupied with the delicate work of healing and did not need a rebellion in her digestive tract. That settled it in a way no principle had.

He felt the loss, though. Standing at his locker before last period, he worked through what he was actually doing with this cooking project, and it seemed to him there were two versions of himself in it. One was the economizer, the boy who portioned and stacked and planned, who believed a system could protect you from waste and chaos. The other was the one who cut corners when he was tired, who assumed the freezer was magic because magic was easier than attention. He didn't think the second boy was gone. He suspected that boy would cut a corner again some Tuesday when he was hungry and lazy, and he couldn't say for certain which version would be holding the spoon that day. What he had, for now, was a rule he actually understood instead of one he'd invented.

That evening he took the suspect container out, looked at it under the kitchen light, and dropped the whole thing, chili and plastic, into the bin outside, because even washing it indoors seemed like pushing his luck. His mother called from the couch to ask what he was doing out there in the dark. "Throwing out a lesson," he said, and came back in to start the rice.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: At the same interest rate, a longer loan term lowers the monthly payment but increases the total interest paid over the life of the loan.
story:
The dealership sat behind a thin arboreal screen of maples that did nothing to muffle the highway, so Luca heard the trucks even inside the glass showroom, where a blue hatchback rotated slowly on a platform like something being proved. He was seventeen, and he wanted that car, or a car, any car, because the bus to his summer job took fifty minutes and the drive took eleven. His father stood beside him with his hands in his pockets, saying nothing, which was his way of saying everything.

Zavier had come along for the ride, mostly because he liked showrooms and partly because he'd spent two years maligning Luca's family for never buying anything, as if frugality were a character flaw rather than a habit. "There he is," Zavier said, spotting the blue car. "Ask about the payment. That's all that matters. Can you make the payment or not."

A salesman with a lanyard and a warm handshake led them to a desk and slid a sheet across. Sixty months, five percent, three hundred and twelve dollars a month. Luca did the multiplication in his head, slowly, twice, because the number that came out was not the price of the car. It was the price of the car plus thousands more. When he said so, the salesman nodded without embarrassment, the way a person agrees that water is wet. "Interest," he said. "That's the cost of borrowing."

Then the salesman offered something better, or something that looked like better. He turned the sheet over and wrote a new figure: seventy-two months, same five percent, two hundred and sixty-eight a month. Lower payment. Luca felt the relief arrive before the suspicion did, and he watched the two of them circle each other. "And the total?" he asked. The salesman tapped at his calculator, unhurried, and turned the screen around. The total was bigger. Lower payment, longer road, more paid by the end.

"That's an oxymoron, right there," Zavier said, pointing at the paper. "A cheaper payment that costs more." Luca said it wasn't, technically, it was just arithmetic being patient, but he kept his voice low because his father had leaned in and was reading the sheet the way he read bills at the kitchen table, top to bottom, twice.

While the men talked numbers, Luca's phone buzzed. A message from Ms. Friedman, his neighbor, who had sold him her old lawnmower business's client list last spring and paid him, quietly and generously, into a savings account he'd opened at her suggestion. "Watered your money tree today," she wrote. "Deposit posted. They added the interest. It's small now. It won't always be. Same idea as your father's mortgage, only pointed the other way." He read it twice, then looked up at the showroom ceiling and thought about interest flowing in two directions, one of them feeding him and one of them feeding the bank, and how a person could stand at a desk like this one and choose, poorly, which current to swim in.

His father asked for the sixty-month sheet back and folded it into his jacket. "We'll think about it," he told the salesman, which they both knew was a no, or at least a not yet, and Luca felt the specific disappointment of a want deferred by exactly the right argument. Outside, in the lot, Anastasia pulled up in her mother's dented sedan to give them a ride home, honking once, and Zavier jogged toward the car calling that he'd told them so, though it was unclear what he'd told them or whether it had been this.

On the drive back Luca opened his banking app and looked at the savings account, at the line where interest had been added, at the small green number doing its slow work. He didn't know yet whether he would wait a year and buy something used with cash, or take the shorter loan in the fall, or whether his father would change his mind entirely. The maples thinned and the highway opened up. "Eleven minutes," Anastasia said, checking the clock as she merged. "You'd have loved that."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Steelmanning is the practice of restating an opposing argument in its strongest form, even stronger than the other person put it, before responding to it.
story:
The motion on the board read: This house believes that a cosmopolitan education is worth the cost of leaving home. Noemie had drawn the closing rebuttal, the slot Ms. Chowdhury called "the grave digger," because a good closer buried the other side's case and salted the earth. She sat at the front table with her flow sheet, and across from her Mahee was whispering to Kael, both of them smiling in the way people smile when they think they have already won.

The first speaker for the opposition was Kael. He argued that telling students to become cosmopolitan, at home everywhere and therefore, he claimed, rooted nowhere, was a kind of theft. You could not send a girl eight thousand kilometres from her grandmother's kitchen and call it enrichment, he said, and then quote a statistic about global competitiveness as if the statistic were the whole of the matter. The room liked it. Noemie watched the judges' pens move, and she wrote on her sheet: emotional anchor, family, cost of distance. Then, underneath, in smaller letters, because she was honest even with herself: he is not wrong about the grandmother.

Mahee spoke second. Her argument was cooler, almost geometrical, about the epistemology of debate itself: that you could not weigh "worth" without first delimiting what counted as a cost, and that the proposition had smuggled in a definition that made their side unanswerable. If any homesickness counted as a cost, and any broadening counted as a benefit, then the debate was rigged before it began. Noemie felt something snag in her, a small hook of recognition. She had built her own case the same way, choosing definitions that made her conclusion inevitable. It was effective. It was also, she thought, a little like winning a race you had drawn the track for.

During the preparation bell she went to the washroom and stood with wet hands, looking at her notes. Her second speaker had already delivered the prepared material, all of it aimed at the weakest version of Kael's argument, the straw man they had rehearsed in practice: that the opposition were sentimental provincials afraid of the world. But Kael had not said that. He had said something harder, about the specific weight of a specific kitchen, and if she answered the version she had prepared instead of the version he had given, the judges would see it, and Mahee would see it, and she would deserve to lose.

She remembered her father in September, over the forms for residence. She had wanted to argue, had loaded her arguments like stones in a pocket, and then, half to stall, she had said: "You're afraid that if I go, I'll come back someone you don't recognize, and you'll have lost me slowly instead of all at once." He had gone quiet. He had said, "That's better than I said it." The conversation after that had not been a fight at all. She had forgotten, in the months since, that she had done that on purpose.

Back in the hall, she stood for her rebuttal. "Before I respond," she said, "I want to state the opposition's case, and I want to state it as well as it can be stated. Better, maybe, than it was." She laid it out: that a cosmopolitan ideal asks people to pay in the currency of intimacy, that the cost is not sadness, which passes, but erosion, which does not, and that a benefit measured in opportunity is being weighed against a cost measured in people, and the scale itself, as Mahee showed, has been rigged. She turned to Mahee. "You're right that we defined 'worth' to suit ourselves. I concede the definition. I'll argue on yours."

She heard a judge stop writing and look up. The hall had gone the quiet that comes when the audience stops rooting and starts listening. She argued that even if costs were counted generously, a person who understood two homes could hold a loss without being destroyed by it, that breadth and depth were rivals but not murderers of each other. She did not fully believe the last part. She said it anyway, because it was the strongest available form, and she had promised herself she would only ever answer the strongest available form.

At the break, Ms. Chowdhury crossed the hall, coffee in hand, and paused at her table. "That restating you did," she said. "That's called steelmanning." She walked on before Noemie could answer.

The judges split two to one, for the opposition. Kael gathered his papers and came over, and Noemie braced for the gloat. Instead he said, quietly, "Your version of my grandmother argument was better than mine. Can I use it at regionals?" She laughed, and then stopped laughing, because Mahee was holding up her flow sheet, on which she had written, in the margin, a single line: watch out, she does to us what she did to us. "Next round," Mahee said, "I'm going to steelman your case before you can. Then where will you be?" Noemie began to answer, then looked down at her own notes and found that every line she had written against them was already, line by line, the best thing anyone had said all day for their side.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: For Mexico's Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2, families build home altars called ofrendas with orange marigolds, whose bright color and strong scent are believed to guide souls home.
story:
Jade stood in the doorway of the cultural center holding her grandmother's photograph in both hands, the way you hold something that could be ruined by a single drop of rain, though it had not rained in weeks. Behind her, her mother was still parking the car, and ahead of her the hall had been transformed overnight into something neither quite church nor quite party. Long tables ran the length of the room, stacked with pan de muerto and mandarins and clay saints, and over everything hung the smell of marigolds, so thick and sweet it was almost a sound.

She had not wanted to come. That was the honest version. She had wanted to spend the afternoon at Paris's, where nobody would ask her to explain anything, and where grief was a private thing you were allowed to skip. Her mother had said only, "Your abuela's picture should be there," and Jade, who at eighteen had lately discovered the pleasure of arguing, had found she could not argue with that sentence.

Paris had come anyway, uninvited and on time, which was its own kind of loyalty. Now she drifted beside Jade through the crowd, reading the printed signs taped to the pillars. "What are these called?" she asked, gesturing at the tiered altar where families were arranging photographs, candles, and armfuls of orange flowers.

"Ofrendas," said a woman arranging sugar skulls, without looking up. "Offerings. You put out what they loved, and the flowers bring them home." She lifted a marigold toward the light. "Cempasúchil. The color and the scent, they say, guide the souls back. That's why November first and second smell like this all over Mexico."

Jade had assumed, in the parochial way of someone who had grown up half inside a tradition and half outside it, that the flowers were decoration, that the whole apparatus was decoration, a costume the past wore. She had even said as much to Paris on the drive over, something dismissive about folklore, and Paris, who was kind enough not to relish being right, had said nothing at all. Now, watching a man her father's age set down a tiny bottle of mezcal and then stand with his hand resting on it, Jade felt the floor of her certainty shift. Decoration did not require a man to stand like that.

Her mother found her by the altar, out of breath from the parking lot, carrying a plastic bag with candles and a dish of her grandmother's molletes. "Put her up there," she said, and when Jade hesitated, because the top tier was crowded and she did not want her grandmother wedged between strangers, her mother added, "Second level. Next to Tío Beto." There was a protocol, Jade realized. There was an order to this that she had never bothered to learn, and not learning it had felt, for years, like freedom, and now felt like something closer to having been quietly disenfranchised, cut out of a vote she had never known was being taken.

She placed the photograph. The frame was brass and cold, and she steadied it against a jar so it faced the room, and then, because the woman with the sugar skulls was watching and because it seemed suddenly important, she took a stem of marigolds from the basket and laid it at the base of the photo. The scent rose up at her, stronger at close range, almost unbearable. Her grandmother had grown marigolds along the fence in the old house; Jade had forgotten this, or filed it somewhere inaccessible, and now it returned entire: the fence, the hose water on the leaves, her grandmother snapping off dead heads with her thumbnail.

Paris appeared at her elbow with two paper cups of cinnamon coffee. "You okay?" she asked, and Jade said, "I told you this was just for tourists," and Paris laughed and said, "You did," and neither of them said the rest, which was that Jade had changed her mind and was standing in the middle of the proof.

Her mother lit the candles and then stood with her hands folded, doing whatever she did silently, and Jade understood that she did not have to join it, and understood also that not joining it had a different weight now, a weight she could choose or choose against, knowingly, for the first time. Whether the marigolds actually guided anyone anywhere, she could not say and did not need to say. What she knew was that for the length of one afternoon her grandmother would be looked at, spoken to, fed in effigy, and that this was a kind of reprieve from the ordinary silence, in which the dead simply stayed gone and no one said their name out loud. She took the coffee from Paris and drank it, and the steam drifted toward the photograph, and the marigolds went on burning their impossible orange under the hall's fluorescent lights.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
story:
The library's heating had been set for winter, though it was only October, and Juliette had unzipped her jacket within five minutes of sitting down. She had claimed the table by the window on the second floor, the one with the view of the parking lot and the sycamore that dropped its leaves in a way she found disorganised, and she had spread her materials in front of her like evidence for a case she was not sure she wanted to win: a laptop, a folder of drafts, and a printed decision page with a single line of small text she had read eleven times.

Aydin dropped into the chair opposite her with a coffee he was not supposed to have on the second floor. "You're checking the portal again."

"I'm not checking it. It's open. Those are different activities."

"What's it say?"

"Nothing. It says nothing, which is its whole personality."

Aydin had his own want, which was a summer research position at the university lab, and he had already applied twice and been waitlisted once, a fact he mentioned with the careful casualness of someone testing whether the word waitlisted stigmatized him or merely described him. He turned his phone face up, then face down, then face up again. "Ophelie's coming. She went on a campus tour yesterday, the actual college, the one you applied to. She has information."

"Information," Juliette said, "is a strong word for anything Ophelie reports."

Ophelie arrived eight minutes later, still in the tour sticker, which she had not removed, possibly deliberately. She sat down and leaned across the table. "Okay, so the guide was doing the whole pitch, the fancy dining hall, the tree that's older than the country, and then he says, and I quote, our yield is one of the highest in the region. And this dad in front of me raises his hand and asks what that means."

Juliette closed her laptop halfway. "What does it mean?"

"So the guide says it like it's obvious. Yield is the percentage of students a college admits who then accept the offer and enroll." Ophelie said it in the guide's exact cadence, a little smug, a little rehearsed. "And everyone nodded like they'd known it their whole lives."

Juliette opened the laptop again and stared at the decision page. The nothing on it had not changed, but it looked different now, and she disliked how quickly it looked different. "So if their yield is high," she said slowly, "it means when they say yes, people say yes back."

"That's what the dad said. He said, so it's like a popularity contest, and the guide got very polite about it."

Aydin leaned forward, which was how Aydin signaled a theory. "So think about it from their side. They're not just deciding if they like you. They're deciding if they think you'll come. You're applying to eleven schools. They know that."

"I applied to nine."

"Nine, eleven, it's a mood. The point is they're guessing about you while you're guessing about them."

Juliette sat with this. It rearranged something she had been carrying for months, this idea of the application as a judgment being handed down from a height, and she did not entirely like the rearrangement either, because it meant the people on the other side were also uncertain, also doing pragmatics, running the numbers on strangers. She had wanted to be chosen cleanly, for reasons she could respect. The possibility that she might be a percentage in someone else's spreadsheet was less romantic, though possibly more honest.

"I interviewed there," she said. "Ms. Rivera made me practice. She said I sounded too much like I was reading a ransom note."

Ms. Rivera taught her literature class and had, over the years, graded her essays with comments like interesting but evasive, which Juliette had eventually understood was a compliment with teeth. At the end of the interview practice, in the empty classroom, Ms. Rivera had asked her one question that had not sounded like a question: whether Juliette wanted this college or wanted to have gotten into it. Juliette had said both, honestly, because at seventeen she was not yet required to know the difference, and Ms. Rivera had looked at her for a long moment and said, "Fine. Keep both. Just know you're holding two things."

Ophelie was peeling the sticker off her jacket. "Here's the thing, though. The dad asked a follow-up. He asked if the college ever admits people they're sure will turn them down. And the guide said that would lower the yield, and then he laughed like the dad had asked if the dining hall served unicorns."

Aydin sat back. "So they protect the number."

"It's a number they brag about on tours," Ophelie said. "Of course they protect it."

Juliette looked at the window. The sycamore had dropped more leaves, and a man in the lot below was failing to parallel park, pulling out and re-angling, over and over, with a patience that struck her as either admirable or deluded. She thought about the guide's cadence, the smugness of it, and she thought about her own nascent strategy, the email she had drafted to the admissions office about her interest in the linguistics program, which she had not sent because it had felt like begging. Now she understood it as something else. It was information traveling in the wrong direction, a signal that she, the admitted-or-not-admitted party, could send back up the wire. Whether that was more honest or less honest than silence, she genuinely did not know. Both were performances. Silence was just a performance for no audience.

"Send the email," Aydin said, watching her face.

"It's not begging," Ophelie said. "It's yield management."

"It might be begging," Juliette said. "But it might also be true, that I want to go, and the only crime is that I want other things too, and they know that, and I know they know."

She pulled the laptop toward her, opened the draft, and deleted the first sentence, which had started with the word firstly, like a lab report. Behind her, at the front desk, a librarian asked a man to lower his phone call, and he lowered it, and in the window's reflection Juliette could see the parking lot, where the parallel parker, on what must have been his ninth attempt, slid the car neatly into the space at last.

Juliette reread the first line she'd rewritten, then hit send.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle, and he published it in the journal Enzymologia instead.
story:
The bus back to school left at four, which gave Noah exactly fifty minutes inside the museum, and he intended to spend none of them in the gift shop. Lauriane and Braydon had other plans. They peeled off toward the tornado exhibit before the group had fully cleared the revolving doors, and Mr. Murphy, counting heads with the weary patience of a man on his fourth field trip of the term, waved Noah on without a word.

He had a reason for the biochemistry hall that had nothing to do with the unit test. Two weeks ago, the regional science fair committee had sent him a form letter. His project, a table of respiration rates in yeast under different sugar concentrations, had not been selected for the final round. The letter used the phrase "limited scope" twice. He had read it eleven times on the bus and then folded it into his back pocket, where it still sat, soft at the creases.

The hall was nearly empty, all glass cases and dim lighting, as though the designers thought molecules deserved an ascetic reverence. Noah stopped at the model of a mitochondrion, cut away like a dollhouse, its folded inner membrane rendered in cheerful plastic. He traced the pathway with his finger above the glass. Glucose in, broken first to pyruvate, then the slow wheel of the cycle: citrate, then the reshufflings, carbons shedding as carbon dioxide, electrons ferried off to the electron transport chain, and at the end of it all, ATP. He mouthed the steps in order, testing himself, and lost his place twice at the same spot, somewhere between the four-carbon acids, where the names blurred into alphabet soup.

"There's a timeline on the side wall," Lauriane said, appearing beside him with Braydon, who had commandeered two stools from the café and was spinning one under his palm. "Murphy says we have to write something up or the trip doesn't count for anything."

"I'm not writing about the tornado," Braydon said. "I've seen a tornado. It's basically a big drain."

Lauriane drifted toward the wall, and Noah, still stuck on the cycle, followed her more out of habit than interest. The wall was a chronology of discovery, small panels with photographs and short paragraphs. She stopped at one and read it twice, her lips moving slightly, and then she looked at Noah with an expression he couldn't parse.

"Wasn't your thing the yeast energy thing?" she asked.

"Rejected thing. Yes."

She tapped the glass. He read the panel. In 1937 Hans Krebs worked out the citric acid cycle, the very wheel Noah had been trying to memorize, the wheel that turned in every aerobic cell on earth. The journal Nature rejected his paper on it. Enzymologia published it instead. Krebs later received the Nobel Prize for the work. Noah read the panel a third time, slowly, and something in his chest went quiet and strange, the way a room goes quiet when a noise you had stopped noticing finally stops.

"That's the cycle," he said. "The one in the model. That exact one." He pointed back toward the dollhouse mitochondrion. "Nature said no to it."

"Nature the journal," Lauriane said, and almost smiled.

Mr. Murphy's voice came down the hall, announcing the bus, announcing it again with less patience. Braydon spun the stool one final time and let it wobble to a stop. Noah stood there a moment longer, the folded letter still in his back pocket, and understood that he was holding two things that did not fit together easily: a rejection was real and it stung, and the same work, the same mind, could be refused by the most respected gatekeepers and still be true. He could not make those two facts resolve into a comfortable lesson, and he suspected that anyone who could was lying. What he had was a yeast project nobody had wanted and a pathway he now knew cold, step by step, because a man the journals had turned away had traced it first.

At the doors, the group was already bunching toward the parking lot. Braydon asked what he'd been staring at, and Noah took the letter out of his pocket, unfolded it once, and dropped it in the bin beside the revolving doors.

"Tell you on the bus," he said, and pushed through into the afternoon light.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the second derivative test, if f'(a) = 0 and f''(a) is negative, the function has a local maximum at x = a.
story:
The bell over the door of Pham's Market had been broken since June, so Leah announced herself by the squeak of her sneakers on the tile. She carried her calculus binder under one arm and a two-dollar coin in her fist, and she set both on the counter beside the register as though they were equally negotiable.

"You're early," Mr. Pham said. He was crouched behind the coffee station with a soldering iron, finishing the repair he had begun at noon. "Lucca not with you?"

"He's coming. He had to print something." Leah unfolded her homework against the impulse cooler, where the humming glass kept the page from sliding. The problem was f(x) = x³ minus 12x, and the question wanted the local maximum, and Leah had gotten as far as the derivative, 3x² minus 12, and then as far as x = 2 and x = negative 2, and there she had stopped, because the two numbers looked exactly alike to her and only one of them could be the peak.

Mr. Pham stood, wiped his hands, and looked at the clock with an appetite she recognized. His granddaughter had a piano recital at seven, and his wife was already dressed, and the part-time clerk had called in sick, which was how Leah had ended up with the evening shift in the first place. "When Lucca comes, you two watch the till," he said. "Nothing complicated. I cauterized the leak in the freezer line, the coffee's fixed, and if the lottery machine jams, just unplug it."

"Go," Leah said. "We've got it."

The store at that hour had a strange liminality to it, the way it held both the last of the afternoon and the beginning of the night, school kids drifting out with chips while the streetlamps came on outside. It matched her own position exactly, she thought, one week past graduation and one week before orientation, and she put the thought away because it was the kind that made her melancholic and slow.

Lucca arrived with pages still warm from the library printer and a bag of gummy worms he did not pay for until Leah cleared her throat at him. Then he leaned over her binder, chewing, and read her work. "You found the critical points," he said. "Now you're stuck."

"I don't know which one's the top of the hill," Leah said. "They both make the derivative zero. That's all the first derivative tells me, that the slope flattens out. It doesn't say whether I'm standing on a peak or down in a valley."
