Lucca turned her pencil around in his fingers the way he did when he was deciding whether to give something away. "Second derivative test," he said, and nothing more, and slid the pencil back to her, which was typical of him, offering a doorway instead of a room.

Leah stared at the page. She differentiated again, almost by reflex, and got 6x, which struck her as almost insultingly simple after everything else. Then she substituted. At x = 2, the second derivative was 12, positive. At x = negative 2, it was negative 12, negative, and she felt something click into place, the way the freezer door had sealed itself shut behind Mr. Pham's soldering iron. If the curve was bending downward at that point, if the second derivative came out negative there, then the point had to be the top. "Negative two," she said aloud. "That's the local maximum. The slope is zero there and it's bending down."

"Which is why I park my bike on the hill side of the street," Lucca said, and she laughed, and a customer came in wanting cigarettes, and Leah rang them through on the register she didn't fully trust, counting the change into a palm freckled like her grandmother's.

She was honest with herself about what she still didn't know. She had followed the test the way you follow a recipe, and she could not yet have said why the bending decided the shape, only that it did, and whether that was enough understanding to carry into a college classroom in September was a question she left open on the counter beside the two-dollar coin. Lucca, meanwhile, had his own want: he slid a job application form across to her, the one Mr. Pham kept under the till, and tapped the blank line for weekday evenings. "Somebody has to cover when you leave," he said. "Might as well be somebody who knows where the maximum is."

The streetlights were fully on now. Mr. Pham's car pulled out of the lot with its headlights sweeping the window, and inside the store the coffee machine gurgled, steady and repaired, while Leah picked up her pencil again.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Raising the temperature for an exothermic reaction decreases its equilibrium constant, while raising it for an endothermic reaction increases the constant.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and hot extension cords, and every folding table had been pushed into rows with the optimism of people who believed sixty projects could fit in a space built for basketball. Jordyn set her display board down carefully, checked that the cork balls on her molecular models had not bounced loose in the bus, and began taping her data table to the front edge where the judges would see it first. The table was the whole argument: three trials of the same reaction at three temperatures, with the equilibrium constant calculated for each one. At 25 degrees the K values sat around 340. At 45 degrees they had fallen to 180. At 65 degrees, 96.

"Those are going down," said Emerick, leaning over from the next table, where his project on water filtration looked like a swamp in a box. "Isn't temperature supposed to make reactions faster?"

"That's kinetics," Jordyn said. "This is equilibrium. Different conversation."

"That's what you say about everything."

She smoothed the tape with her thumb. She had noticed the downward slide two nights ago, sitting on her bedroom floor with a calculator and a cup of tea going cold beside her, and her first reaction had been that she'd made an arithmetic error, because everyone knew heat was supposed to help. Then she'd checked a reference table in the back of her chemistry textbook, found the same reaction listed there, and watched the K values fall in the printed column exactly as they fell in hers. The reaction was exothermic. That word, which had always sounded vaguely medical to her, apparently meant the heat sat on the products' side of the ledger, so when she raised the temperature, the whole equilibrium shifted backward, away from products, and the constant itself got smaller. Raising the temperature of an exothermic reaction decreased its equilibrium constant. She had underlined it twice and then felt slightly cheated, because the universe had not bothered to warn her.

Her problem now was simpler and worse: the judges would ask her to predict, on the spot, what would happen to some reaction she had never seen. Ms. Bianchi, her chemistry teacher, had made a show of it in class last week, holding up a card with a made-up reaction and saying, "Suppose I heat this, Jordyn. Which way does it shift?" Jordyn had given a noncommittal answer about "depending on conditions," and Ms. Bianchi had smiled the way she smiled when a student had almost understood something, which was somehow worse than frowning.

Eugene arrived at ten past nine with a bag of clementines and no project, having entered the fair as a volunteer judge's assistant, a role that appeared to consist mainly of handing out badges and eating clementines. "So explain yours to me," he said, peeling one. "I want to be devastated by your intelligence before the judges are."

"It's about pressure," Jordyn said. "Not air pressure. The pressure a reaction is under when you change the temperature. If the reaction gives off heat, heating it is like pushing against something that already has too much. The equilibrium constant drops." She tapped the column. "If a reaction takes in heat instead, an endothermic one, it goes the other way. The constant rises."

"So heat is bad for hot reactions and good for cold ones," Eugene said.

"I'm going to pretend that's not what I said."

The first judge came through at eleven, a man with a lanyard and a pen he never used. He looked at her board for forty seconds, asked her to define equilibrium, and moved on. Jordyn found herself starting to ruminate on the forty seconds, replaying whether she'd said "dynamic" soon enough, and made herself stop by rechecking her arithmetic for the fourth time. The numbers held. There was a steadiness in that, a small unglamorous mercy: the data was not impressed by her anxiety either way.

Ms. Bianchi appeared at noon, when the gym had gone loud with the sound of parents pretending to understand things. She stood in front of the table with her hands clasped behind her back, which was her listening posture.

"You found the trend yourself," she said. It wasn't a question.

"In the textbook table. After my own numbers did it first."

"And what will you do when a judge hands you an endothermic reaction and asks for the direction?"

Jordyn looked at her table, then at the small graph beside it, the one with the K axis and the temperature axis and her three points marching downhill. She thought about the reverse graph, the uphill one she had sketched on a napkin at home, the one for reactions that drank heat instead of sweating it. Two pictures, mirror images, both true, and the only way to know which one you were in was to know which direction the heat flowed.

"Then the constant goes up," she said. "Opposite slope, same principle. Though I'd want the sign of the heat before I'd bet anything."

"You'd want it, or you'd need it?"

"Need it," Jordyn said. "Everything else I could guess at. That part I can't."

Ms. Bianchi nodded once, which was her version of applause, and drifted toward Emerick's swamp.

The second judge arrived at one, a woman with a laminated sheet of questions, and after the third question she pulled a card from her pocket: a reaction Jordyn had never seen, an equilibrium with heat listed on the reactant side, and the question "Predict the effect of raising T on K." Jordyn read the side of the equation where the heat sat, felt the small click of the two pictures lining up, and said, "It rises. Endothermic. The constant increases." She caught Eugene's eye across the aisle; he was holding a clementine half up like a tiny trophy.

The judge wrote something down, and the pen squeaked against the lanyard.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Arabic newspapers across many countries are written in Modern Standard Arabic rather than local spoken dialects, so one written form serves readers in different regions.
story:
Marcus spread the newspaper across his grandfather's kitchen table, smoothing the crease with the flat of his hand. The assignment from Ms. Nguyen was due on Friday: read a short news article in Arabic and summarize it aloud for the class. He had chosen one about a flood in a country he could not immediately place, and now he sat with his finger under the first line, sounding out words that refused to arrange themselves into anything he recognized.

"Read it to me," his grandfather said, setting down two glasses of tea. "Slowly."

Marcus read. Halfway through the first sentence his grandfather laughed, not unkindly, and tapped the page. "Nobody talks like this," he said. "Not me, not your grandmother, nobody at the market. Where did you learn to read like a radio announcer?"

"I don't know what half of it means," Marcus admitted. "That's the problem."

Last summer came back to him unbidden: sitting on the back steps with his grandmother, shelling fava beans into a dented bowl while she taught him the words for everything within reach, the door, the beans, the neighbor's obstreperous dog that barked at every passing motorcycle. She spoke to him the way she spoke to everyone, and within a month he could bargain at the vegetable stand and argue about football. He had assumed, without ever putting it into words, that this was the language, whole and complete, and that reading it would be a matter of learning the letters.

His grandfather leaned over the article and read the headline aloud, quick and fluent, and Marcus heard the difference at once. The same mouth, the same voice, but the shapes of the words had shifted, formal and slightly distant, like a man putting on a good jacket. His grandfather read it the way Ms. Nguyen had read the sample sentences in class, and nothing like the way he ordered bread on Saturday mornings.

"It's the newspaper way," his grandfather said. "The same in the paper in Egypt, the paper in Morocco, my paper here. One written way for everybody." He shrugged. "We speak how we speak, each place its own. We read this."

Marcus copied the headline into his notebook. "So when I summarize for the class, do I do it in the newspaper way or the way you talk?"

"Which one do you actually know?"

"Yours. Mostly yours."

His phone buzzed on the table. Alexe, from class: are you doing the article thing? I found a video of a guy reading it, should I copy his accent? Marcus typed back that he was at his grandfather's and would figure it out, then put the phone face down. Kieran had sent something too, a photo of his own article with half the words circled, and the message this is impossible, they never taught us these words. Marcus looked at his circled page, then at the flood article, and understood that the problem was not his alone.

He had been prepared to give up on the spoken words entirely, to memorize the written article phonetically like a piece of music and deliver it without comprehension. That had seemed easier, and safer. Now he tried something else: he read the first paragraph silently, decoded it word by word with his grandfather hovering nearby, and then, covering the paper, said aloud in his grandmother's dialect what he thought it meant. Some of it came out wrong. Where the article had a word for "damage" that belonged to no conversation he had ever had, he said "the water broke things," and his grandfather nodded and gave him the formal word again, and Marcus wrote both in his notebook, one beneath the other, dialect on top like a translation living inside the original.

They worked through the article that way until the tea went cold. When they reached the end, his grandfather made him stand and deliver the whole summary as if to a room, and Marcus did, stumbling once at the part about the hospitals, where he mixed a formal verb into a spoken sentence and heard his grandfather wince and grin at the same time. He thought of the shelled beans, of how his grandmother's vocabulary had covered a kitchen and a street but never a flood in another country, and how the newspaper's words covered countries he might never see but no kitchen at all. Two ways of speaking, and he was standing in the gap between them, not sure yet whether the gap was a problem or a bridge, or both.

On Friday, Ms. Nguyen called him to the front. Marcus took a breath and began in the newspaper's opening words, then let the rest come out the way his grandmother talked, and watched her tilt her head, listening.

"Where is the rest of it from?" she asked.

"My grandfather's kitchen," Marcus said.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people.
story:
Ryder had written eleven pages, and on page one a family moved into a yellow house, and on page three they planted a garden, and by page six the father was gone and the mother was selling the house and the brother was at a bus station in Reno. He printed it out at the camp office before lunch and carried it to the black box theatre like something hot.

"Eleven pages," said Gillian, weighing the stack in one hand. "Ten-minute play. You've written a miniseries."

"It's the whole summer," Ryder said. "It only makes sense if you see the whole summer."

Gillian was sprawled across two front-row cushions, her own script, four pages about a girl who finds a drowned bee in a swimming pool, tucked under her elbow. She had opinions and no embarrassment about having them. "There's a handout," she said. "Day one, the blue one, you doodled on it." She dug into her backpack, unfolded it, smoothed the crease with her palm, and read aloud: "A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people." She looked up. "So that's that."

Ryder took the handout and read it himself, as though Gillian might have invented the sentence to spite him. The paper said the same thing. Around them the black box smelled of paint and the dust the mop never reached, and Camelia was on the stage taping out a kitchen with blue tape, three boxes on the floor, a doorway that led nowhere.

Ms. Santos-Reyes came through the rows of folding chairs with her coffee and did not sit down. "Ryder, how's it coming?" She said it the way she said everything, like she had all afternoon and also none of it.

"Good," he said. "It's long."

"Mm," she said, and kept walking. She never fixed anything for you. Camelia said Ms. Santos-Reies believed you learned more from a problem than a solution, which Camelia pronounced like a philosophy and Gillian pronounced like laziness, and Ryder privately thought it was a little of both.

That afternoon he sat in the taped kitchen and tried to choose. The summer had six locations: the yellow house, the new apartment, the bus station, the garden, the car, the lawyer's office with the ficus in the corner. Six places, and the handout said one. He could feel the argument forming in him, that life was spread out like that, that you couldn't cram it into three boxes of blue tape. He could also feel the argument losing.

Here is what Gillian saw, because after lunch she had decided to watch him instead of working, the way you watch someone carry too many groceries: Ryder sat inside Camelia's taped kitchen with his knees up, reading his own pages and tearing some of them out. He tore out the yellow house. He tore out Reno. He read one page a long time, folded it small, and put it in his pocket, and then he laughed at something, alone, which looked either very good or very bad.

"You okay?" Camelia called from the light booth.

"I killed the garden," Ryder said.

"Murderer," she said. "We barely knew it."

What survived was this: eleven thirty at night, the kitchen table, the boy supposed to be asleep, coming down for water and finding his father packing a duffel bag at the table, quietly, the way you pack when you've already decided and you're only finishing the deciding. Two characters. One setting. The whole summer inside one duffel bag if he could get it there. He worked through the afternoon and skipped the improv game and ate a granola bar in the dark of the house seats, and by dinner he had a draft in which the father kept saying "It's not about you" and the boy kept asking questions that were not really questions.

At the read-through, Camelia played the father, because Camelia could do a grown man's tiredness better than anyone at camp, and Gillian read the stage directions in a bored, nonchalant voice that somehow made them funnier, and Ryder played himself, which he had thought would be easy and was not. His line "Do you want me to help you fold that" came out wrong twice, too flat, and he understood that he had written a boy who was calmer than he had been, a boy who offered to help fold the shirts instead of standing in the doorway with a glass of water he never drank. He had made himself better, and now he had to decide whether to put the worse boy back in.

"That's the ending?" Gillian said afterward, flipping the last page. "He helps fold the shirts and the dad leaves?"

"That's the ending."

"It's good," she said, which from Gillian was nearly a standing ovation, and then, because she was Gillian: "It's also a lie, right? You didn't help fold anything."

Ryder considered denying it, then didn't. "I wanted to," he said. "I don't know if that counts."

Ms. Santos-Reyes passed behind them on her way to lock the booth and paused just long enough to say, "Friday you stage it," and was gone before he could ask her the question about the lying, whether making yourself kinder on paper was the same as being kinder, or whether it was a way to expiate something you hadn't done, or whether it was just what an aesthete did with a bad night, made it beautiful and called it enough. She would not have answered anyway. She would have said "Mm."

Friday, the lights came up on three boxes of blue tape, a table, a duffel bag, and Camelia in a man's jacket, folding a shirt slow, like it was the last shirt in the world. Ryder stood in the taped doorway with an empty glass and waited for his line. Somewhere out past the lights, Gillian was reading his stage directions in that flat voice, "He does not drink the water," and he let the glass hang in his hand and heard his own voice come out younger than he had rehearsed it, and the boy on the page and the boy at the table sat down together at last and began to fold.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: A Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible, noticing servants and workers the novel mentions only in passing.
story:
The assignment was due third period, and Alexia was doing it on the school bus, which everyone knew was a lie she was telling herself. Ms. Shin had handed out a single chapter of Pride and Prejudice and two questions: whose labour keeps these people comfortable, and how does the novel treat it? Alexia had underlined nothing. She had, however, eaten half a bag of pretzel nuggets.

"I don't even know what I'm looking for," she said, sliding across the green vinyl seat as Kurtis got on at the second stop. "You've read it."

"You've read it too. Last year. You wrote a whole essay on irony."

"Irony is easy. Irony is just people being wrong in a fancy way." She tapped the photocopy. "This is asking me to see what's not here. How do I look at a hole?"

Kurtis dropped his backpack between his feet and considered this with the seriousness of a boy who liked problems more than answers. "Then count what is here," he said. "That's what my sister does with her lab stuff. When you can't see the thing, you count everything around it."

So Alexia counted. She went through the chapter with the stub of a pencil, making a small tick every time a servant appeared, even in passing. A footman. A maid sent with a message. The man who drove the carriage. Somebody's laundry, delivered by an unnamed pair of hands. By the time the bus lurched past the hardware store she had nineteen ticks, and beside them, in a second column, a record of how many lines those nineteen people actually spoke. Zero. Not one word. A whole invisible workforce, and the novel let it carry trays and open doors and then dissolved it like sugar in tea.

"Wait," she said, gripping his sleeve. "Nineteen servants. Zero lines. That's the whole point. The Bennets don't cook, don't clean, don't even drive themselves anywhere, and the book just glides over whoever does all that. It mentions them only in passing. Like furniture that breathes."

"You've gone pale," Kurtis said.

"I've gone right. Like, politically." She laughed, and her heart did that fluttery palpitate thing it did when an idea actually landed, the same feeling as nailing a serve in gym class. "This is what the lens is. It's not about hating the characters. It's about asking who's under the floorboards."

"Ms. Shin is going to love you," Kurtis said. "She's going to make that face."

But then Susan got on at the light by the pharmacy, saw the ticks, and complicated everything, as Susan did. "You could flip it, though," she said, wedging in across the aisle. "Half those ticks are people choosing to work, aren't they? Darcy's housekeeper in the next chapter, Mrs. Whatshername, she's proud of the family. Not everybody's a prisoner."

"Okay, but she still doesn't get to inherit anything," Alexia said. "Pride is not a wage."

"Pride is not a wage," Kurtis repeated solemnly, writing it on his palm. "That's going on the bathroom wall at school."

Alexia chewed the end of her pencil. She felt the two arguments circling each other in her head, and for a moment she wanted to just pick one, because picking felt like being done. Ms. Shin always said a good essay holds a position, and Alexia, a complete neophyte at criticism, had assumed that meant a fortress you defended with your whole body. But sitting there with the bus's heater rattling under the seat, she began to suspect it was more like a bridge you built while admitting the river was still moving underneath. She could count the servants. She could notice the silence. She could also admit she didn't know, from nineteen ticks, whether any of those people were miserable. The chapter wouldn't tell her. That was exactly the kind of hole she'd been trying to look at.

"Here's my position," she said slowly. "The comfort in this book is real comfort, and real people made it, and the book can't see them. But I can't invent what those people felt either. That'd just be me putting words in their mouths the way the novel wouldn't. So my argument is the counting, and the honest part is that it stops there." She paused. "Is that allowed? Can an essay stop somewhere and wave?"

"Ms. Shin calls that a limitation," Susan said. "She loves limitations. She says it's what grown-up thinking smells like."

"That is tangential and also disgusting," Kurtis said, and Susan kicked his backpack.

The bus swung into the school loop, gears complaining, and Alexia wrote her last line in the margin while her stomach did a small nervous flip: nineteen mentioned, zero heard, one reader changed. Not bad for a neophyte on a bus. She underlined it twice, then remembered her rule about not trusting herself, and crossed out changed, and wrote it again anyway.

They funnelled down the steps into the cold. Through the gym doors she could see Ms. Shin arranging chairs, and Alexia stood a second on the frozen gravel, papers against her chest, breath hanging in the air.

"Third period," Susan said. "Go get your wave."

"I'm going," Alexia said, and started across the lot before she could change her mind.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of rubber mats and the coach's coffee, and Benjamin had been pushing the weighted sled for exactly one practice, one miserable hour, before he noticed something odd. Alone, at the start of the session, each of them had pushed the sled the full width of the court, grunting, thighs burning. But when the coach made them push in threes, the sled barely moved faster, and nobody even seemed tired. The coach blew his whistle and said the word "pathetic" twice, which everyone agreed was a personal best.

"Maybe the sled gets heavier when it's lonely," said Cedrik, lying flat on the bleachers afterward like a man felled in battle. "Like it grieves."

"Maybe you get lighter," said Jimmy. "You've been absconding from effort all season, honestly. I saw you. You were hiding behind my pushing."

Benjamin said nothing, because he was busy having a thought, which for him was a physical event, like swallowing something sideways. He had read about a French engineer, Maximilien Ringelmann, who published a paper in 1913 about people pulling on a rope. Each person in a group pulled less hard than the same person did pulling alone. Benjamin had filed it away under "things I will never use," a morass of a folder that also contained the melting point of butter and the number of teeth in a shark. Now, sitting on the gym floor with his shoelace between his fingers, the fact floated up out of the swamp and tapped him on the shoulder.

He tested it quietly, without announcing anything, because announcing things to Cedrik and Jimmy was how ideas got laughed to death. At the next practice, when the coach split them into rope teams for the tug-of-war conditioning drill, Benjamin watched. Cedrik, alone on the dyno machine earlier, had pulled like a man trying to drag a piano out of a burning building. In the group, gripping the same rope as three others, Cedrik's face went calm, almost serene, the face of someone enjoying a hedonistic afternoon rather than fighting for his life. It wasn't laziness exactly. It was something quieter, something that happened to everyone, even, Benjamin suspected, to himself.

"I saw that," Benjamin said afterward, toweling his neck.

"Saw what? I was pulling."

"You were holding. Jimmy was pulling. There's a difference, and it has a name. Ringelmann. French engineer, 1913. People pulling rope in a group each pull less hard than they do alone. Every single one of us. It's not an insult, it's a finding."

"You're telling me science proved I'm a slacker," Cedrik said. "In 1913. Before I was even born. That's efficient."

"Before any of us were born," Jimmy said. "Which means our grandfathers were also slackers. It's hereditary. You can't fight genetics, Benjamin."

Ms. Fischer, who taught physics and supervised the gym on Tuesdays mostly to escape the teachers' lounge, had overheard the word Ringelmann from the equipment room doorway. She did not explain anything, because explaining was against her religion. She only raised her eyebrows at Benjamin and said, "Library has the translation, if you're serious," and went back to counting dodgeballs, and Benjamin understood he had just been handed something without being told what it was.

He thought about it through the rest of the week, dribbling a ball in his driveway in the dark. The team wasn't bad because they were weak; they were bad in groups. So maybe the answer wasn't to try harder together, which the coach kept yelling at them to do, his voice going up an octave each practice like a kettle. Maybe the answer was to be alone together: each man with his own rope, his own count, his own sled to push across that gleaming gym floor, shoulder to shoulder but not hand over hand. Or maybe that wasn't the answer either. Maybe you lost something when you stopped pulling the same rope, something you couldn't measure with a dyno machine, and the trick was holding both ideas at once without pretending either one was the whole truth. He didn't know yet. He suspected he wouldn't know until the last game of the season, and maybe not even then.

At Friday's practice the coach split them into rope teams again, and Benjamin picked up his end, and Cedrik picked up his, and Jimmy wrapped the rope twice around his fists like a professional. Before the whistle, Benjamin leaned forward and said, "Pull like it's just you. Just you and the rope, nobody else on it."

Cedrik grinned, set his feet, and said, "If I pull my own weight, does that make me the load or the engine?"

The whistle went, and the rope went taut.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
The repair shop smelled of solder and warm plastic, and the fan in the corner turned its torpid circle without moving much of anything. Katherine set her phone on the counter, screen webbed from the corner outward, and watched Mr. González tilt it under the lamp. Behind her, Colton leaned against a rack of charging cables, scrolling with his thumb in the quick, hungry way he had when something was about to be everywhere.

"You have to see this," he said, and turned his phone toward her. On the small screen a river of animals moved across a gray savanna, dust rising behind them, and beneath it a caption claimed the footage was from a wildlife reserve flooding that morning. Three hundred thousand shares already. "I'm posting it to the group chat. Everyone's freaking out."

"Wait," Katherine said. Her mother was picking her up in twenty minutes, before the shop closed at six, and there was no room in that window for a long argument, but something about the clip itched at her. The light in it looked wrong for morning, or the animals moved like a different season, and she could not have said which, only that she noticed it. "Don't send it yet."

Colton rolled his eyes. "It's literally on the news page."

"It's on a page," she said. "That's not the same thing."

Mr. González looked up from her phone. "New screen will take me fifteen minutes," he said, which meant she was standing there with nothing to do, and Colton with his thumb hovering, and the video spreading the whole time like something left too long in a warm place, fermenting in the dark of a thousand group chats.

She took his phone, opened the search engine, and typed a description of the clip, and got nothing useful, a wall of unrelated hits. Then she tried what she thought people meant by a reverse image search, dragging the video link into the search bar, and the engine refused it flatly. She tried a second one and it refused her too. "It won't take a video," she said, more to herself than to him. "Image engines can't search it directly. That's the whole point of reverse search, and it just won't take it."

"So it can't be checked," Colton said. "Great. Sharing."

"No." She scrubbed the video backward and forward until she found a frame where the lead animal filled the shot, its horns sharp against the dust, and she paused there and took a screenshot. Then another frame, mid-herd, and a third of the flooded bank. She dragged the first screenshot into the image search, and after a slow turn of the loading wheel, results bloomed across the screen: the same picture, the same animals, the same horns. The oldest result was dated three years back, on a photographer's portfolio, captioned in a language she didn't read, tagged with the name of a different country.

Colton leaned in beside her, and she could feel the moment when he stopped arguing, the way a person goes quiet over a wrong answer they can see clearly. "That's the same herd," he said.

"Frame by frame, that's how you do it," she said. "You can't search the video, so you search the frames." She ran the second screenshot and got the same answer, different pages, same three-year-old animals walking through a dry season that had nothing to do with any flood. She did not know who had recaptioned the clip, or why, or whether the flood itself was even real somewhere else under a different camera. That part stayed open in her, unsolved and a little cold.

Mr. González called her name and held out her phone, the new glass unmarked, catching the fan's slow air. She paid him, and Colton stood there holding his own phone in both hands, the post drafted, his thumb not moving. From outside came the sound of her mother's car pulling to the curb, two minutes early, and Colton deleted the caption line and typed a new one at the top of the clip: "This is from three years ago, not today."

Katherine pushed through the door into the evening, and behind her she heard him say, to the group chat or to nobody, "Okay, but how did nobody else catch that?"

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind a car, so a quick look over the shoulder is needed before merging or changing lanes.
story:
Eli had measured out the parking space twice with his mother's car, using the front edge of the bank's brick wall as a reference point, and both times he had ended up a foot from the curb. The lot behind the bank was empty on Saturday mornings, which was the whole reason he'd chosen it, that and the fact that Ms. Reddy, who lived in the apartment above the branch, had told him the security cameras only recorded the front.

"You're looking at the wall again," Kaeden said from the passenger seat, phone flat on his knee. "You're supposed to look at the rear tire."

"The wall helps me."

"The tire helps you. The wall is a guess with a building attached."

Eli pulled forward, reversed with his hand over the passenger seat, and came in crooked again, the rear wheel a hand's width from the curb, angled like something abandoned. He let the car sit there. Through the windshield he could see the drive-through lane, the pneumatic tube that carried deposits into the building, and beside it Nahla, sitting on the concrete bumper with a folder of paperwork, waiting for her mother to finish a refinance inside. She waved with two fingers, not looking up from her forms.

"She's been there since nine," Kaeden said. "Her mom's trying to consolidate loans before the interest jumps." He said it lightly, the way he said most things, but there was something underneath, and Eli, who had known him since seventh grade, could hear it. Kaeden's family had done the same thing last spring, and afterwards Kaeden had stopped driving to school in his dad's car. It was not a subject. It was more like weather that had passed over and left the ground different.

"Set me up again," Eli said.

They ran it four more times. On the fourth, the right rear tire kissed the curb with a sound like a knuckle on a door, and Eli felt something loosen in his chest, a small and probably premature satisfaction. "That's a pass," Kaeden said. "Barely. Do it once more so it isn't luck."

The second time Eli did it clean. He sat with the engine idling, hands on the wheel, and Kaeden clapped his shoulder once, twice. "Road test is Wednesday. You have the parking. Now the merge, because the merge is where they fail you." Kaeden wanted the merge done today, Eli knew, because Kaeden had a plan for after: highway out to the outlet mall, a specific store, a jacket he'd been describing for a week. He needed Eli licensed, and Eli needed him anyway, so the arrangement held without either of them naming it.

The on-ramp rose in a long curve toward the interstate, and Eli accelerated into it the way the booklet said, matching the speed of traffic. He checked the mirror. Empty road, silver and afternoon-bright. He signalled and began to drift left, and then something in him, some borrowed instinct, turned his head, and there was a grey sedan almost beside him, close enough that he could see the driver's mouth moving. Eli corrected, held his lane, hands shaking on the wheel.

"Blind spot," Kaeden said. "Mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind a car. You have to look over your shoulder." His voice was flat, not scolding. "The mirror showed nothing. The car was still there."

Eli drove in silence for a mile, the grey sedan easing ahead and disappearing. He had trusted the mirror completely, the way he'd trusted the wall for parking, one fixed reference for a moving world. The wall had half worked. The mirror had told him a confident lie, or rather, it had told the truth about what it could see and he had heard more than it said. He thought about Ms. Reddy's cameras, seeing only the front of the bank, the rest of the lot presumed rather than known. It seemed to him that a person could ossify around his own angles of vision, could let a single way of looking harden into the whole of looking, and that this happened so gradually it felt like simply being careful.

"Do it again," he said.

The next on-ramp was three exits up. This time Eli checked the mirror, signalled, and turned his head sharply over his left shoulder, a motion that felt, the first time, like abandoning the road entirely, like an act of faith that the windshield would still be there when he came back. The lane beside him was clear. He merged smooth as pouring water.

"That's it," Kaeden said. "That was actually it."

They drove on. Nahla had texted a photo of the bank, her mother still inside, the folder now closed. Kaeden mentioned the jacket again, the store, the price, and stopped himself. Eli said he'd drive him there Wednesday, after the test, if he passed, and Kaeden said nothing for a moment, which was its own kind of answer.

At the last exit before home, Eli took the loop down, and in the curve he glanced at the side mirror, at the road behind, and then, deliberately, over his shoulder, into the small blind country where things travel beside you, unseen and close, going the same speed you are.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: Germany uses a constructive vote of no confidence: the Bundestag can remove a chancellor only by electing a successor in the same vote.
story:
The sign taped to the double doors of city hall read MODEL PARLIAMENT, ROOM 2B, and beneath it, in smaller print, a reminder that food was not permitted, which Kobe took personally, since he was eating a bagel as they climbed the stairs. Jackson had been assigned Germany. This was supposed to be a privilege, the teacher said, a country with a system worth studying, but mostly it meant Jackson had to explain why nobody in his faction could simply fire the chancellor the way the Americans impeached a president, which Zoe kept suggesting they do, loudly, every five minutes.

The room was set up like a chamber, rows of folding tables, a card table for the speaker, and Mr. Owusu, the civics teacher who had organized the whole thing, sitting at the back with a thermos and the expression of a man who had learned not to intervene unless blood was drawn. Jackson held the folder of research he had done at the library the night before, photocopies with paragraphs highlighted in three colors because he could not decide which paragraphs mattered.

Zoe opened the session by moving to remove the chancellor, who was a boy from another school wearing a blazer that suggested he had practised being chancellor at home. "I move that we have no confidence in this government," she said, and sat down with the satisfaction of someone who believed she had just accomplished something.

"Seconded," said Kobe, through the bagel.

Jackson stood, and this was the part he had rehearsed in the shower, except in the shower nobody was watching. He said that in the American presidential system the legislature could remove a president without installing a replacement, the vice president stepped in, the office survived on its own. But Germany, he said, and here he checked his highlighter colors against his memory, was different. The Bundestag could remove a chancellor only by electing a successor in the same vote. It was called a constructive vote of no confidence. You could not just say no. You had to say whom instead.

"That's rigged," Zoe said immediately.

"It's the opposite," Jackson said. "It means you can't collapse the government out of spite. You have to have someone ready."

The chancellor in the blazer inclined his head, the judicious tilt of a man who had not expected to be defended by his opposition. Zoe argued that a rule forcing you to name a replacement was a trap, because what if the replacement was worse, and Jackson found himself agreeing with her more than he wanted to. He had spent an hour the night before trying to titrate the two systems against each other, weighing stability against accountability, and he still could not say which he would choose if anyone asked him to choose. The presidential system let you throw out a bad leader and sort out the aftermath later. The parliamentary one made you do your sorting first. He trusted one procedure more and the other outcome more, and he had not yet worked out how to hold both opinions in one head.

Mr. Owusu came forward and offered them a deal, or something like recompense for wasting their Saturday: if the chamber could not agree, the two systems would be run side by side, the same crisis, two procedures, and the room could watch where they diverged. Zoe got her American impeachment. Jackson's faction got the German rule, the same vote, the successor named inside it. Kobe was appointed vice president, a role he performed by eating a second bagel that was not, technically, his.

They ran it twice. In the American version Zoe won, the chancellor was removed, and the chamber spent twenty minutes arguing about whether Kobe was now in charge, which Kobe neither confirmed nor denied. In the German version nobody could agree on a successor, the vote failed, and the blazer survived, smug in a way Jackson found almost admirable. Between the rounds Zoe leaned across the aisle and said she still thought her way was fairer, and Jackson said he still thought his way was safer, and neither of them conceded, which felt, privately, like the most accurate result of the day.

When the room emptied at four, Mr. Owusu collected the signs and the folding tables and told Jackson, on his way out, that the chancellor in the blazer had been the one to request Germany as his country, because he had read about the rule and liked his odds. Jackson stood in the doorway of room 2B holding his folder of three-colored highlights, and watched the boy in the blazer descend the marble stairs of city hall, unhurried, into the afternoon.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, the closest relatives of the person who died sit shiva, a mourning period of seven days that begins after the burial; the Hebrew word shiva means seven.
story:
The ground was soft from three days of rain, and the men from the funeral home had laid plywood over the grave so the mourners would not sink. Daniel stood between his mother and his uncle, holding the small shovel they passed down the line, and watched the first clod of earth strike his grandfather's coffin with a sound like a fist on a door. His grandfather had been a pelagic fisherman in another life, before the move, before the hardware store, and Daniel had always pictured his death as something out on open water. Instead it happened in a hospital corridor that smelled of disinfectant, and now it was ending in a cemetery off Route 9 with a highway humming behind the fence.

Daniel had something to say, and no moment to say it in. All week he had been rehearsing a single sentence, something about the summer they had spent mending nets, and he had assumed the graveside would be the place for it. But the rabbi spoke, and the shovel went around twice, and then everyone was walking slowly back toward the cars, and the sentence was still in him like a stone. He told his mother he would catch up. She looked at him a long moment and let him go, which he understood was its own kind of permission.

He stood at the edge of the grave after the others had gone. The plywood was still down, the mound of earth beside it waiting, patient as anything. He had it in his head that grief should feel like weather, something vast that presaged itself, that gave you clouds before it gave you rain. What he felt instead was smaller and more practical: he owed a man a sentence, and the man was now underground, and the debt had nowhere to go.

Behind him, gravel crunched. Yuvraj was coming up the path in the dark suit he wore for debate tournaments, carrying a paper bag from the bakery on Main Street.

"You're still here," Yuvraj said. "Everyone's at your house already."

"I know. I needed a minute."

Yuvraj set the bag down on the grass. "My mom sent babka. She said you don't bring flowers, you bring food. I didn't know if that was right."

"It's right." Daniel looked at the bag, then at his shoes. "We're not going back to a normal house, though. That's the thing nobody told me. The closest relatives sit shiva. My mom, my uncle, me. It's seven days, and it starts after the burial, so it's starting right now, basically. That's what shiva means. Seven."

"So I showed up on day one."

"You showed up exactly when you're supposed to." Daniel had learned it that morning, from his cousin's phone in the waiting room, scrolling while his mother signed papers. Sitting shiva. Seven days, the closest relatives, low stools, mirrors covered, doors open to visitors. No one had explained it to him directly. He had pieced it together the way you piece together anything that is about to happen to you, half from reading and half from watching his uncle drag the dining chairs down to the living room floor.

"I don't know what to say to your mom," Yuvraj said. "That's the honest answer. I've been standing out here for ten minutes working on it."

"Don't say anything good. That's what the rabbi said this morning. People kept trying to tell my mom he was in a better place and she kept going kind of rigid. Just say you're sorry and then stand there. Standing there is the whole job."

Yuvraj picked the bag back up. "My dad's a pragmatist about everything, you know. He said, bring food, don't stay long, don't ask questions. I thought that was cold. Now I think it might be the kindest thing anyone's told me this week."

They walked out together, past the rows of stones with Hebrew on one side and English on the other, and Daniel realized he was going to have six more days of this, a house full of people eating and standing there, and that he could not decide whether that was a mercy or a sentence. At the cemetery gate his uncle's car was still idling, waiting for him, the rear door held open.

"There's one thing," Daniel said, stopping. "I had this thing I was going to say at the grave. I stood there and I couldn't, and now I feel like I missed it."

Yuvraj shifted the bag to his other hand. "You've got seven days."

Daniel got in the car. As they pulled out onto the road, his mother turned around from the front seat and looked at him, and she was not crying, she was holding a covered dish someone had pressed on her and looking, for the first time all week, almost amused.

"You went back to the grave," she said. "Your grandfather did the same thing at his mother's funeral. Forty-five minutes. Everyone stood around eating without him."

"I'm not going to make a habit of it," Daniel said.

"You already have," she said. "That's exactly what he said."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Ontario requires most private residential landlords to use a government standard lease form for new leases, and a tenant can request one in writing if it was not provided.
story:
Jasmine spread the two leases side by side on the bus stop bench, weighting the corners with her phone and a flat stone she'd found in the gutter. The 52 bus came every twenty minutes, which gave her exactly enough time and no more. One lease was for a room in Mael's cousin's house near campus, fourteen pages of small print and a rent of nine hundred and twenty dollars. The other was a basement apartment she'd found online, seven hundred and fifty, all inclusive, the ad said, which Jasmine had already learned could mean anything.

"What happens if hydro isn't included," Mael said, dropping onto the bench beside her with two coffees. He slid one across. "Because that basement looks damp. Damp means a dehumidifier. A dehumidifier means the meter spins."

"That's why I'm doing this here instead of at home." She flipped to the utilities section of the first lease, ran her finger down it. "At home my mom just says don't sign anything, which is not actually a strategy. Heat and water included, hydro capped at forty a month, tenant pays the rest. So I call the utility company for last winter's bills, add that, plus internet, she's splitting it, whatever, fifty each." She wrote the numbers in the margin, pressing hard enough to dent the next page. "Nine twenty plus maybe forty plus fifty. Over a thousand."

"And the basement?"

"No utilities at all. Seven fifty means seven fifty. But." She held up the second document, and something about its first page had been bothering her since the showing yesterday. It wasn't the price or the clause about no guests after ten. It was the paper itself. The first lease had a government-looking header, a form number in the corner, checkboxes about smoking and parking. The basement lease looked like something the landlord had typed himself on a Sunday, with his name in bold at the top and a line at the bottom that just said "one year, then month to month."

"Maybe. But there's a thing, I read it somewhere and I can't remember where. Hang on." She texted Bodhi, who was the kind of person who read the whole tenant board website for fun, and while she waited she kept adding numbers, because the numbers were the part she could control. Renter's insurance, twelve a month for the room, quoted this morning. The basement landlord hadn't mentioned insurance at all. Laundry, four dollars a load at the rooming house, but the basement had a machine, and she calculated it out, roughly two loads a week, and felt briefly, absurdly exhilarated by the fact that she could put a price on her own sock washing now. That was a kind of power. Small, parochial, a power that extended no further than this bench and this decision, but power.

Bodhi texted back a link. Jasmine read it twice, then a third time, her lips moving. "There it is. Ontario has a standard lease form, the government one, the one Mael's cousin used. Landlords have to use it for most private residential rentals, new leases. And if you don't get one, you can ask for it in writing." She looked up. "In writing. That's the part. You send a letter, an actual written request."

"So the basement guy just didn't bother?"

"Or didn't know. Or knows." She turned her phone so Mael could see the screen, though he was pretending to be more interested in the traffic. "The point is I don't have to guess which it is. I ask in writing and I find out what kind of landlord he is before I hand him a deposit."

The 52 rounded the corner, and she gathered the pages fast, folding them into her bag with the numbers facing inward like a secret. Mael stood, then didn't get on. "Wait," he said. "I changed my mind about something. Yesterday I said take the basement because of the price. But you're going to be eighteen in a house where the guy doesn't even use the right form, and I know you, you'll spend the whole year fighting him and calling it character building." He hesitated, and she saw what it cost him, because Mael's whole position on everything was that feelings were optional and math was not. "The room costs more. I ran it too, last night. But it costs more the way a door with a lock on it costs more."

"Mr. Teo would say something about false economies right now."

"Mr. Teo says a lot of things. Most of them are right and that's the worst part."

Jasmine laughed, and then stopped, because the bus was idling and the driver was watching them in the mirror with the patience of a man who had seen every variety of teenage hesitation. She still didn't know what the basement landlord would say to a written request. She didn't know if the hydro bills would come in at forty or sixty, or if her mother would sign the guarantor line without a speech about how she'd said don't sign anything. The uncertainty sat in her chest like a held breath, but it was her uncertainty, attached to a decision she was making with arithmetic and a legal form she'd found herself.

She stepped onto the bus and took the aisle seat, and Mael followed, and before the doors closed she was already drafting in her head: Dear Sir, I am writing to request the standard Ontario lease form as required for new residential leases.

"Send it tonight," Mael said.

"Send it tonight," she said, and typed the first line into her phone, right there, while the streetlights came on outside the window.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
The Coleman stove had two burners and one temperamental knob, and Brayden had claimed both by the time the sun dropped behind the pines. He had planned the dinner for two weeks: chicken thighs seared in the cast iron pan, rice with the last of the dried mushrooms, a tin of peaches for after. His father had done the driving and the tent and the fire ring, and Brayden had said, at the door of the house before they left, that he wanted to cook the whole meal himself this time. His father had looked at him a moment longer than necessary and then said fine.

Now the thighs were hissing, and Tiger, who had begged his own way into the trip because his parents were repainting the apartment and he refused to spend three days breathing fumes, sat on the cooler with a paperback he was not reading. Tiger's actual want, he had confessed on the hike in, was to get his phone back. His mother had confiscated it after a fight about a C in chemistry, and his plan, as far as he could articulate one, was to be so pleasant and useful all weekend that his father, who was picking him up Sunday, would vouch for him. He had already carried Brayden's pack up the last hill without being asked, which was how Brayden knew the plan was serious.

Brayden cut into the largest thigh with his pocketknife, the way he had watched his father do a hundred times, looking for pink. The juice ran clear near the surface but the meat near the bone looked faintly rosy, and he could not decide whether that was undercooking or just the way thigh meat was. He pressed the knife in again. He thought about the argument he'd had with Aydan in the library in June, Aydan insisting that eyeballing food was how humans had done it for ten thousand years and Brayden insisting that ten thousand years of food poisoning was not exactly a recommendation. Aydan had called his attitude rationalism, as an accusation, and Brayden had taken it as a compliment, and neither of them had resolved anything, which was usual.

"Stop stabbing it," his father said, coming up from the water spigot with the wash bucket. He set it down, dug in the plastic bin of kitchen gear, and produced a slim digital thermometer in a yellow case. Brayden had packed that bin himself and hadn't known it was there.

"Where'd that come from?"

"Your mother." His father held it out. "She said, and I quote, chicken is safe at one sixty-five. You stick it in the thickest part and wait for the number."

"One sixty-five what?"

"Fahrenheit. Seventy-four Celsius, if you ever cook for the rest of the world." His father shrugged and went back to the dishes, and the instruction hung there, complete and unembellished, the way his father preferred things.

Brayden slid the probe into the thickest thigh, careful to avoid the bone, and watched the digits climb: 141, 149, 158. He thought of Aydan again, and of his own certainty in the library, and found that the two positions were not, in the end, opposed. The thermometer was rationalism in a useful, small form, but his hands still had to know where the thickest part was, still had to judge the sear and the rest, and all of that was the vestigial knowledge his grandfather had cooked by, not useless, just incomplete. He could hold both. The screen settled at 167, and the rosy meat near the bone, he understood now, was something he would never fully settle by eye, and that was fine; the number settled it.

"Okay," he said, mostly to himself. "Okay, they're done."

Tiger set down his unread paperback. "Can I plate them? Your dad said if I actually helped he'd talk to my mom before we leave." He was already up, already reaching for the chipped enamel plates, arranging them with a formality the camp table had never seen, folding paper towels into napkins and laying the forks at angles. Brayden watched him fuss and felt an unexpected tenderness toward the whole transparent scheme.

They ate in the lantern light, Tiger charming Brayden's father with questions about his old truck, the chicken so good that his father took seconds and then, without ceremony, thirds. It was only afterward, scraping the pan, that Brayden found the thermometer still lying on the cutting board, never washed, its yellow case snapped shut by Tiger's tidying hands. He held it under the spigot, dried it on his shirt, and when he opened the case to check he hadn't killed it, the screen lit up and read, in patient gray digits, 74.

"Celsius," Tiger said, leaning over his shoulder. "See? Chemistry."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA advises refrigerating cooked food within two hours, or within one hour if the air temperature is above 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit).
story:
The community kitchen smelled of onions and dish steam by ten in the morning, and Sebastian had a clipboard he was trying to treat like something more important than a clipboard. On it he had sketched the week: chili on Monday and Tuesday, rice and beans Wednesday, a tray of baked chicken stretched across Thursday and Friday. Ms. Wilson, who ran the kitchen on Saturdays, had told him that planning was the hard part, that cooking was just following through, and he was beginning to understand what she meant. The morning clouds had already burned off, thin and gray, adumbrating the heat that would settle over the parking lot by noon.

"You've got protein twice a day all week," Chantelle said, leaning over his list. "That's more than my whole family manages." She said it lightly, but she said it twice more while they chopped, and Sebastian had learned in the past month to notice when Chantelle repeated a thing.

He portioned the chili into containers, then the rice, labeling each lid with blue painter's tape. The system was his own invention, and he was quietly proud of it. His mother worked evenings now, and the plan was that she would come home to a fridge with dinners stacked in it, nothing to decide at eleven at night except which tape to pull. That was the want underneath all the chopping: not to learn to cook, exactly, but to hand her one less thing.

August arrived at noon with a borrowed cooler and an argument already half-formed. "The van's in the shop," he announced, "so everything rides in my trunk, and we eat lunch at the picnic tables before we load up. It's too nice to eat inside."

It was too nice, which was the problem. They carried the pots out anyway, and the chili and the leftover chicken from a practice batch sat on the folding table in the sun while they ate sandwiches and argued about whether August's cousin had actually dunked on Mr. Reyes in the church league game. Sebastian had a presentiment, small and specific, that he was forgetting a number. He kept glancing at the pots, gleaming in the light, while August did an acerbic impression of a referee who had apparently never seen a travel in his life.

Back inside, washing the sandwich board, he found the sheet Ms. Wilson had left in the folder she'd given him his first day. He'd read it once and filed it away. There it was in plain print: the USDA advised refrigerating cooked food within two hours, or within one hour if the air temperature was above 32 degrees Celsius, 90 degrees Fahrenheit. He looked at the thermometer suctioned to the window. It read 34.

"Everything's been out since noon," he said. "It's been over an hour, and it's above thirty-two."

Chantelle stood very still with a towel in her hands. "So lunch chili is done? The whole batch?"

"The whole batch that sat out. Two hours is the rule normally, but when it's this hot, one hour." He was already carrying the pots to the sink, tipping the chili into the compost bin, steam rising sour and paprikaed into the air. August came in and saw the empty pot and the tape labels stacked uselessly beside it.

"Man," August said. "That was your Monday and Tuesday."

"I know what it was." Sebastian rinsed the pot longer than the pot needed. Then he stopped, because Chantelle had pulled the clipboard toward her and was reading his week, and she said, "There's still the rice and the beans we never took out. And if we start a new chili now, it's two hours to cook and we cool it tonight for Monday. You'd only lose Tuesday." She looked at him, not at the pot. "And I'm free till five."

They cooked the second chili together, August dicing peppers without being asked, Chantelle adjusting the heat because Sebastian's chili always came out timid. Somewhere in the stirring, Sebastian understood that his clipboard plan had assumed a world where nothing sat out, where vans didn't break, where heat was an abstraction, and that the real skill wasn't the plan but the readiness to remake it. What he couldn't yet say, even to himself, was whether he'd have remembered the sheet at all if the thermometer hadn't been on the window, and he decided that was a question for next Saturday.

At four, the containers went into the blast chiller Ms. Wilson had shown him, tape relabeled, Tuesday marked TBD. He carried Chantelle's bike out of the hallway so she could leave, and August honked twice from the lot, windows down, sun still heavy on the asphalt.

"Next week," Sebastian called after them, "we eat inside."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle in his 1704 book Opticks, an early version of the color wheel artists use today.
story:
By the time the bell rang for the last twenty minutes of class, Andrew's canvas still had a hole in the middle of it, not a literal hole, but a blank patch where the sky behind his brother's silhouette refused to become anything. The project was due at the end of the period. Ms. Pelletier had said it twice that morning, once kindly and once not, and now she moved between the easels with her clipboard, pausing at each one like a doctor making rounds.

"You're going with orange and blue," Jeremie said from the next easel, not asking. "Complementary. Safe."

"It's not safe. It's just right." Andrew squeezed cadmium orange onto his palette and immediately regretted it, because the orange he imagined and the orange in front of him were two different colors, and he did not know how to get from one to the other. He wanted the painting to feel the way the lake felt at six in the evening, warm at the horizon, cold where the water took over, and he only had the vocabulary of a kid who had learned everything he knew from one semester of videos.

Kade leaned over from the window side, brush behind his ear. "You could just do what I did. Make it all moody and dark and tell her it's about loss." He held up his own canvas, which was mostly gray. "Teachers love loss."

"Teachers love a color scheme that holds together," Ms. Pelletier said from across the room, without looking up.

Andrew pulled out his phone, which was technically against the rules, and typed Newton color wheel, because that was the one thing he half remembered from somewhere, a diagram of colors bent into a ring, and he hoped the ring would tell him what to do with his sky. The screen gave him more than he expected. Isaac Newton had arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle, and published it in 1704, in a book called Opticks. He read the sentence twice. Not a painter. A physicist, drawing a circle of light three hundred years ago, and somewhere between that circle and this classroom it had become the thing artists used.

"Did you know the color wheel started with Newton?" he said, still holding the phone. "1704. He put the spectrum in a circle in his book Opticks. It was an early version of the one we use."

"Bro, we have fifteen minutes," Jeremie said.

"I know. That's not the point." But it was partly the point, because the deadline was pressing on him the way deadlines do, making everything feel both more urgent and less important at once. Newton's circle put red opposite green and blue opposite orange, and Andrew's instinct had been to run orange into blue at the horizon, and the circle said that instinct was a kind of collision, not a blend. Yet the lake at six in the evening did run orange into blue, and it was beautiful, and no circle explained that. He sat with the two ideas for a moment, the system and the evening, and neither one yielded.

He decided not to accede entirely to the wheel. He mixed a grayed violet, the color halfway between his two enemies, and laid it along the horizon where they met, so that the orange arrived through it and the blue arrived through it, and the transition belonged to neither side alone. It was not grandiose. It was a narrow band of paint, maybe two inches, and it would not impress anyone who wanted a sunset screaming off the canvas. But it was a considered thing, and he could say why he had done it, and he could also say what he still did not know, which was whether the painting worked or whether he had only made his confusion tidy.

"Five minutes," Ms. Pelletier said, and the room filled with the sound of brushes being rinsed too fast.

Jeremie came around the easel and stood in front of the canvas with his arms crossed, doing his best impression of someone with discernment. He looked for a long time. "The middle part," he said finally. "Where it goes through that purpley gray. That's the good part."

"Ten minutes ago you called orange and blue safe."

"Ten minutes ago there wasn't a middle part." Kade appeared beside him, gray canvas tucked under his arm, and they both kept looking, and Andrew picked his brush back up, dipped it in the violet, and extended the band a little farther along the horizon, into the part of the sky he had been most afraid of.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: On Mexico's Day of the Dead, orange marigolds called cempasúchil decorate altars and graves, because their bright color and strong scent are thought to guide the souls of the dead home.
story:
Isla found the list on the refrigerator on Thursday morning, in her grandmother's slanted handwriting, though her grandmother had been dead for nine days. Marigolds, it said. Sugar. Little skulls made of paste, the kind her grandmother always bought from the Mexican grocery on Alder Street instead of making herself. Below the list, in her mother's newer, straighter hand: I'll do the altar. You do the flowers.

"I'm not doing the altar at all," her mother had said the night before, scraping rice into a container nobody would eat from. "I'm setting out a photo and calling it enough." She said it like a decision, but her voice had a crack in it, and Isla had gone upstairs without arguing, which for her was its own kind of surrender.

The problem was the flowers. Isla had walked to Alder Street with forty dollars of grocery money in her pocket, expecting buckets of marigolds the way there were buckets of roses before Valentine's Day, and instead the grocery had a single crate of them, orange and ragged, already picked over by women who had come earlier and known what they wanted. There were also white chrysanthemums, cheap and plentiful and pretty, and Isla stood between the two for a long time, holding her phone in one hand without texting anyone.

Joel worked the register on Saturdays, and today, improbably, Thursday. "They have to be the orange ones," he said, when she asked him, in the tone of someone reciting something he'd been told rather than something he understood. He reached into the crate and turned one flower toward her, its petals dense and rough as a scab. "Cempasúchil," he said. "My mom says the color and the smell guide the souls home. That's why they're all over the altars and the graves this time of year." He shrugged, embarrassed, as if he'd said too much.

"Guide them home from where?"

He didn't know. He was seventeen and worked at a grocery store and his knowledge ended where his mother's sentences ended. Isla bought the last bunch of orange ones, eleven dollars, and then, with the change, a bundle of the white chrysanthemums, without deciding exactly why.

Jayda came over that afternoon, because Jayda came over most afternoons and did not seem to register that a house with a dead grandmother in its recent past might want quiet. She flopped onto the kitchen chair with her history homework, and when Isla mentioned the Day of the Dead altar her mother was half-building on the sideboard, Jayda looked up. "We did this in Mr. Wilson's class last year," she said. "He called it a critique of, like, American grief culture. We hide death and they throw it a party." She was quoting; Mr. Wilson had a lot of sentences that got quoted afterward, deployed at parties and in arguments, secondhand certainty.

Isla trimmed the marigolds under the tap while Jayda talked. The smell came up off the stems, sharp and green and a little like citrus gone wrong, and she thought that if smell really did work like a road, her grandmother's particular soul would want a road of something else: lavender soap, burnt tortilla, the metallic sweetness of the communion wine she took on Sundays. Grief was not a party and it was not a hiding; it was, at the moment, a seventeen-year-old holding flowers over a sink, trying to make an argument to no one.

"You're overthinking it," Jayda said, watching her. "It's flowers. It's a nice thing to do."

"Mr. Wilson problematizes everything, so now you problematize nothing, and you think that's balance." Isla said it without heat, and Jayda laughed, and the conversation dissolved into homework, which was a relief to both of them.

But later, alone, Isla carried both bunches to the sideboard where her mother had put the photograph and, uncharacteristically, gone further: a candle, a small dish of salt, the clay bird her grandmother had kept on her windowsill for forty years. Isla set the marigolds in a glass of water in front of the photo, their orange loud against the wood, their smell rising, warm and strident, filling the corner of the room. Then she stood there with the white chrysanthemums in her other hand.

She thought about her philosophy elective, the unit on existentialism, the claim that nothing carries meaning until a person puts it there. If that was true, then the marigolds guided souls home because enough people, for enough generations, had decided they did, which made the belief both arbitrary and unbreakable, a rope woven from nothing that could still hold real weight. Her grandmother had believed in that rope, or half believed, the way she believed in saints and in the lottery and in the medicinal power of Coca-Cola. And Isla's mother believed in nothing so far as Isla could tell, except exhaustion, except the photo and the candle and enough.

She set the white chrysanthemums in a second glass beside the first. Not instead of. Beside. The white ones were for the part of her that didn't know, and the orange ones were for the part that wanted, this once, to be guided. It was a compromise that would have annoyed Jayda and slightly saddened her grandmother, and Isla could not have said why it felt like the truest thing she'd done all week.

Her mother came home at six with paste skulls in a paper bag, stopped in the doorway of the dining room, and looked at the sideboard for a long time. She put the bag down. "There are two vases," she said.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The Chicago Manual of Style, whose notes-and-bibliography system uses footnotes, was first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906.
story:
Mia spread her sources across the corner table of the cafe like a dealer laying out a bad hand: three library books, a folded photocopy, and her laptop open to a document titled "draft1_FINAL_final." Emy-Rose slid into the opposite chair with a hot chocolate and peered at the screen.

"How many footnotes do you have?"

"None," Mia said. "That's the problem. Ms. Kerr wants an argument, footnotes, a bibliography, Chicago style. I know how to argue. I don't know how to prove I argued."

"You could just make up a system," Emy-Rose said. "Little numbers, small text at the bottom. Who checks?"

Mia turned the laptop toward her. On the screen was a page of instructions from Ms. Kerr, dense with abbreviations, and beneath it the library's copy of a thick orange book, checked out in Mia's name, its cover stamped with a university press logo. She had carried it around for two days without opening it past the table of contents.

The argument itself she had. Her paper was about a nineteenth-century dissident whose pamphlets had been banned, and Mia had taken a position she could defend: the banning had spread his ideas further than the pamphlets ever did. Mahmoud, in their shared history seminar, had claimed the opposite, that censorship had debilitate the movement he led. Mia had gone home and found, in a footnote of a book she was reading for the paper, a reference to reprint runs in three other countries. She wanted to be right, but she also wanted to be honest about the parts that stayed murky, and the murk was winning.

"Who invented this?" she said now, flipping the orange book open at random. "Who wakes up one morning and decides where the comma goes?"

Emy-Rose leaned over the copyright page and read aloud, her finger under the line. "The Chicago Manual of Style, first published by the University of Chicago Press, 1906." She sat back. "That thing is older than your great-grandparents."

"Older than everybody's great-grandparents," Mia said. But she kept her finger on the page. Nineteen hundred and six. The dissident in her paper had been alive then, printing pamphlets in a basement. Some of his first citations, if he had made any, might have followed rules from that same book, or its first edition, anyway. She felt an odd tenderness toward the orange volume, as if it were a lugubrious old relative who had outlived everyone it had been written for and still insisted on correct punctuation.

Mahmoud arrived with an iced coffee and heard the whole dispute again, twice, once from each of them. He refused to concede the censorship question, but he did concede the footnote question, and the three of them spent twenty minutes building Mia's first citation, arguing about whether the author's name came before or after the title until Mia found the model in the orange book and slapped the table hard enough that the man at the next table looked over his newspaper.

That night the point of view belonged, briefly, to Ms. Kerr, who sat at her kitchen table with a stack of first drafts and read Mia's email twice.

Dear Ms. Kerr, it said. I have an argument but the evidence is uneven. The reprint runs are real, I have them footnoted, but the connection to his later influence is harder to prove, and I would rather say that than stretch it. Also I have a question about the bibliography. Did you know the Chicago Manual of Style was first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906? I found it on the copyright page and it made the whole thing feel less like a rule and more like something people have been doing for a long time, and getting wrong, and doing anyway. My footnotes still aren't all right, I think. Thank you for reading this far. Mia.

Ms. Kerr set the letter aside and wrote a single line on her grading sheet, then crossed it out and wrote nothing, because the draft beneath the email in the stack was not like the email at all. The draft hedged everywhere, buried its argument in the second-to-last paragraph, and cited sources it had not really used. The email knew what the draft did not yet know it was allowed to do.

Two mornings later Mia was back in the cafe corner, the orange book propped against the sugar dispenser, her second draft crawling with small numbers. Emy-Rose found her there at noon, still in her coat, and read the new opening paragraph over her shoulder.

"You moved the argument to the front."

"I moved myself to the front," Mia said. "The argument was always there. It just had to prove it existed." She scrolled to a footnote, deleted it, retyped it. "Some of them are probably still wrong."

"Which ones?"

"I genuinely don't know," Mia said, and typed on.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In the recapitulation, the second theme usually returns in the home key rather than the dominant, so the movement ends settled in the key where it began.
story:
Leo had spread the score of Mozart's Sonata in A major across Ms. Halvorsen's piano bench like a map of a country he was supposed to govern, and so far his reign consisted of two pencil marks and a feeling of dread.
